subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (for the Minister of Finance) moved
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-97, an act to provide borrowing authority, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
She said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to open this debate today on Bill C-97, an act to provide borrowing authority. I should say as a member of the cabinet that it was the borrowing authority bill which was one of my first duties in this House in 1985. I am delighted to be able to introduce this legislation again today, a very important part of government operations.
To begin, it is important to set this bill in the right context, and that is in the context of the economic policies of the government as they were set out last week in the budget speech of the Minister of Finance.

That Budget Speech set out a plan for economic recovery that will lead this country to further growth and renewed prosperity. The key to that recovery is lower interest rates, interest rates which will encourage economic activity.

We are going to bring about those lower rates by doing three things that were identified last week in the House by the Minister of Finance: first, we are going to set clear, achievable inflation targets; second, we will move government finances along the way towards a balanced budget; and, third, we will severely restrain government operations.
Together, these proposed measures are a commitment to effective government management and control, something which will serve Canada well for years to come and which we have followed since we were in office, following many years of neglect.
These measures will tightly control spending. Program spending will be limited to 3 per cent growth per year after 1991-92. They will hold the deficit to $30.5 billion this year and next and, in 1992-93, reduce it to below $25
billion for the first time in a decade. The measures will enable the government to eliminate new federal borrowing in financial markets in 1993-94.
In other words, as we look at the bill before us, we should keep in mind that the measures in this budget will substantially reduce the amount of borrowing authority which the government will need in the future.
The subject of government borrowing, a veiy important one, naturally brings to mind two things which we should consider: the public debt and the deficit. In past periods of recession, governments have typically resorted to additional spending, and suspended their concern about the government's fiscal position. Members opposite who would have us do the same thing today ignore the fact that, in those earlier times, the government was not carrying the burden it does today, a burden of 20 years of persistently high deficits and accumulating debt because Liberal governments increased spending not only in difficult times, to meet emergencies and to promote economic growth, but also in good times instead of cutting back.
I am reminded of the biblical story of the seven years of famine and the seven years of feast when one has to save for the bad times. It is worth remembering that an increase in spending above that proposed in the budget would be directly reflected in the amount of borrowing authority requested in this bill.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: I remember the good old days.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Oh, yes. The good old days that led us into the trouble that we are in today.
Our public debt is forecast to reach $400 billion by mid-year. The interest cost alone will amount to more than $43 billion next year, more than is spent on old age security, unemployment insurance, and family allowances combined.

Our government has been responsible in its approach to this problem. Since coming to office in 1984, we have waged a difficult battle to reduce the deficit and increase our control over the debt. Progress has been made. We have substantially reduced the growth of the debt, and we have halved the deficit as a proportion of national income.
March 5, 1991

In 1989, the Minister of Finance set out a medium-term fiscal goal of bringing new government borrowing in financial markets to an end by 1994-95. This would be achieved by sharply reducing the deficit. This goal was reaffirmed in the 1990 Budget, which included new measures to ensure that it could be reached.
The Budget presented last week proposes further action to ensure that we reach this goal, despite the reduced revenues and higher expenditures resulting from the weak economy, and despite higher debt charges resulting from higher interest rates.

We are extending the existing expenditure control plan, because discipline and sustained restraint of program spending is the key to deficit reduction and debt control. The two-year program announced last year will be extended to a total of five years. Programs subject to this plan will grow at an average annual rate of 1.7 per cent.
There are, of course, some important programs that are exempted, as there should be, and those are the income support programs for seniors, for families and for veterans, unemployment insurance, and equalization. Other exemptions are Canada Assistance Plan payments to lower income provinces and Indian and Inuit programs. These exempt programs, accounting for 60 per cent of all program, spending will grow by an average annual rate of 3.9 per cent over the life of the plan.
Furthermore, we are reforming government management. We are intensifying the restraint that has been in place since 1984, which was so essential at that time and remains essential today, and which has reduced operating costs in real terms over the intervening period.
Salaries of MPs and ministers will be restrained, as will Public Service salaries, including those of executives, deputy ministers and heads of Crown corporations.
Layers of management, built up through inertia over the years, will be removed. The number of senior managers in the Public Service will be reduced by 10 per cent. Capital spending and non-wage operating budgets will be frozen at 1990-91 levels.
Government Orders
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, the government will be taking new steps that will compliment these restraint measures. Spending limits will be legislated to ensure that the budget's spending track will be met.
We will establish a special fund, a Debt Servicing and Reduction Fund, to ensure that all revenues from the GST are directed to reducing the deficit.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: What happened to revenue neutral?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Of course you'd say "revenue neutral".

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: A lot of malarkey.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is definitely not malarkey, this is a significant step forward. Canadians from all walks of life know that we cannot continue to mortgage our future, and they want to make sure that the money we spend will go to reducing the debt that was built up through all those profligate years that came before.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Right on.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I am sure these measures will, of course, have the support of all members of this House and it will bring us on schedule to the point at which new borrowing will not be required. That will be a great day for all Canadians, Mr. Speaker.
These are serious measures and I am really sorry that the members opposite do not regard our fiscal situation as a serious one. They require serious attention if they are to be understood. Nowhere is this more true than in considering their impact on the programs that are offered through my department, through employment and immigration. I want to spend a few minutes talking about those programs now.
There have been a variety of claims made by hon. members opposite about the impact of this plan on unemployed Canadians. Well, I want to assure this House that we have made serious commitments to unemployed Canadians from the beginning and we continue to meet those concerns.
Members have particularly seized on one decision, and that was the reduction of $100 million in the Canadian Jobs Strategy budget. They argued, falsely of course, that the government was leaving the unemployed out in the cold. Nothing could be further from the truth.

Government Orders

After the election of 1984, this government reviewed the hodge-podge of job creation and training programs left by the Liberals. The result of this review was the introduction of the Canadian Jobs Strategy in 1985.
With CJS we streamlined training and employment programs. We moved away from the kind of make-work program which had left participants with no more skills and no more ability to break the unemployment cycle than they had had before.
As members on both sides of this House will know from the experience of their own constituents, CJS programs have improved on those that existed previously-
Programs such as Community Futures have enabled people to create stronger local economies. Job development programming has strongly emphasized the skills trainees can use in the private sector.
Innovative approaches to basic skill training have been developed. To meet the challenges of changing technology, we introduced the Skill Shortages and Skill Investment Programs. These programs have helped young people and women re-entering the labour force.
Two years ago, we had to review our support for training and adjustment programs.

We were not alone, of course, in recognizing this need to restructure the hurly-burly of programs that had grown up over the years: the Macdonald Royal commission, the Forget report, the de Grandpre report, as well as the committee report of this House from the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration in the last Parliament, all pointed in the same direction, that our facilities for the unemployed needed changing.
Canada needed an active labour market policy, and while there might have been some disagreement among all those groups on what the policy should be, there was certainly agreement that the government should lead the way in developing an active labour market policy and that, indeed, is what we have done. We have developed a program that helps workers adapt to changing demands,
not one that assumed that those changes would never happen, which is what existed before.
The result of this review process was the Labour Force Development Strategy which I introduced in this House on April 11, 1989, a program which I think is a major achievement for this government and for the people of Canada. The LFDS has been designed to deal with two problems which have existed for a long time. First, Canadian workers all too often lack the skills to get and keep good jobs, that not only would make them better participants in the labour market, but also give them a more satisfying sense of participation and of looking after their families and their families' futures.
The second is Canadian employers who have jobs but who lack the skilled workers that they need in order to fill those jobs. We find consistently that there are areas where there is a mismatch between the jobs available and the skills of those available to fill them.
Our strategy is based on the idea of partnerships; partnerships with employers, with labour, with education and with provinces and territories in a way that we have not seen before. The federal government cannot shoulder the responsibility of training Canada's workers all by itself. What we can do, however, is work with others to increase the amount and quality of training that does take place to ensure that it is relevant for workers and for employers.
The latest step in developing this partnership was the announcement on January 14 of this year of the Canadian Labour Force Development Board. This body will bring together, for the first time ever in Canada, representatives of labour, business and social action groups to help us improve, among other things, not solely, the training of Canadian workers. What a breakthrough for Canada to be able to build the kind of partnership that is going to be needed in the decade ahead and that had been ignored for so long.
Clearly, a key part of the implementation of the LFDS was improving the unemployment insurance program. We wanted to see UI continue to give income to unemployed workers, but at the same time do more, and to provide active in addition to passive help. We wanted UI to be part of this active labour market program that Canadians need and want so much.
March 5, 1991

To achieve this, of course, under current circumstances, we faced a familiar choice. We could raise taxes to pay for these new programs. We could borrow the money, thereby boosting the sums authorized in bills like the one we are discussing today, Bill C-97, or we could find a better way. As usual, we chose the fiscally sound way. We expanded the active side of UI programming and we asked that employers and workers, those who benefit from unemployment insurance, should carry its cost.
Bill C-21 was finally passed into law last fall, after a year's delay by the Liberals in the other place and it provided for this expanded role in spite, of the usual opposition urgings that less was more. As a result, this year the UI program is contributing $1.4 billion for training, training allowances, and employment assistance for UI recipients, money that will be used to train 45,000 more UI recipients than were trained last year.

So what, then, is the real significance of the reduction in funds for the Canadian Jobs Strategy which the budget calls for?
If we examine expenditures on training, training allowances and employment assistance, we find that this year more, not less, will be spent on these programs.
It is important for members to realize that, as important as CJS is, it is not the only element of the federal government's training and employment programming. As can be seen in the Estimates, the government has seen to it that this year over $3 billion will be spend on training, training allowances and employment assistance; that's $500 million more than was spend last year, and $900 million more than the year before. That's more, not less, help for Canadian workers.

In the case of our decision to raise unemployment insurance premiums, we were faced with another difficult choice. As the Minister of Finance noted in the budget, labour market conditions have produced a greater demand for benefits than we could possibly have anticipated.
The expected deficit in the UI account, therefore, would have required large premium increases in 1993
Government Orders
and beyond to eliminate the accumulated deficit and to pay the interest which would be also accumulating inside the fund on that debt.
The more immediate impact of that deficit would be to increase the current cash flow requirements of the government. Without new premium revenues to offset the deficit, the need to borrow would once again increase, and interest on that borrowing would compound the debt problem that we already face.
This is not a time to postpone difficult decisions. UI premiums should rise now, not later. There will still be a deficit in the UI account, and I want to make it clear that the government will finance that deficit. At the end of the day after all, the government represents the taxpayers and those who pay premiums. While the government will finance that deficit, it will be nowhere near as great as it would have been had we not acted now.
In this, as always, the government has acted prudently. We recognize the many needs that government is called on to serve, but we also recognize that it is a delusion, the notion that we can forever expect future generations to be able to pay for our decisions.
The plan for economic recovery, then, makes choices that will help us to return to prosperous conditions and, at the same time, give back to government the financial health that it needs to do its job properly.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: You are making babies cry.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that when that young child grows up, Canada will be a much better place as a result of the policies which this government has introduced.
It is important that we give back to government the financial health that it needs to do its job properly. We do take that responsibility very seriously.
In the meantime, of course, significant borrowing continues to be necessary, and that is why we are here today.
The provisions of this bill are clear and straightforward. First, there is a provision for authority to cover our anticipated requirement for borrowing to meet the net financial requirements, as stated in the budget in a perfectly straight-forward manner.

Government Orders
The amount requested includes provisions to cover the estimated exchange account earnings and a $3 billion reserve to manage foreign exchange transactions. Together, these amount to a request for authority to borrow $26.4 billion.
I should explain, of course, to members opposite one technical point. The request for authority to cover exchange fund earnings, as in previous years, reflects the fact that these earnings reported in the Public Accounts as budgetary revenues give rise to additional Canadian dollar requirements. That is because they are retained on the account and they are not available to finance government operations.
The $3 billion reserve is the same amount as that requested in borrowing authority bills in the last four years. There is nothing unusual about it.

This bill provides, as usual, that at the end of the fiscal year, in this case March 31, 1992, any unused borrowing authority under this bill in excess of $3 billion will be cancelled. This provision preserves the government's non-lapsing reserve into the next year to accommodate the possibility that new borrowing authority may not be provided before the start of the next fiscal year.
As well, the bill cancels the similar $3 billion reserve granted in last year's borrowing authority, the cancellation being effective on the latter of March 31,1991 or the date this bill comes into force.
I want to remind hon. members that this bill provides a borrowing authority which the government needs to meet its requirement for 1991-92. It is important that it be considered in a timely manner.

Sometimes time is of the essence when borrowing authority is involved. For example, the Government of Canada bond issue to be offered for sale March 12 will use up virtually all of the borrowing authority granted for 1990-91. Day-to-day cash flows are volatile, but we expect it will be necessary to use section 47 of the Financial Administration Act for Treasury bills to be sold in the last half of March.

Until Bill C-97 is in place to deal with the next fiscal year, only short-term debt instruments can be sold, and the government cannot maintain the desired balance of short and long-term debt. This balance is carefully designed to reduce the government's exposure to increases in debt service charges resulting from short-term changes in interest rates.

Mr. Speaker, this bill contains no unusual provision, and the information required to understand it is set out fully in the budget documents and in the Main Estimates. I would, therefore, urge the House to proceed with it as quickly as possible so that new borrowing authority will be in place at the beginning of the new fiscal year, and so the government's regular borrowing program can proceed.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is time for a change, real change. This morning's performance of the President of the Treasury Board was one good example of how we desperately need a change. Yesterday, he promised us answers on the spending of the Spicer commission; yesterday he said: " Wait until tomorrow and we will give you the facts".

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: We are waiting.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
In fact, Mr. Speaker, the Supplementary Estimates that he has tabled today shows that almost $18 million will have been spent by this commission up to the fiscal year March 31.
It is likely that at the end of this process this will go down in history as the most expensive royal commission ever to have sat. Given the nature of the work of the commission, one would not argue that it is worth spending money to try and save this country; but when you have a president who, by his own admission, last night refused to call himself a federalist, you have to ask yourself whether, in fact, the money that the federal taxpayers are spending on the Spicer commission is not simply going down a black hole.
I would like to quote what he said because I think Canadians were shocked and horrified to hear his response when asked the simple question: "Are you-well, let me ask it anyway-are you a federalist?"
March 5, 1991

"I am a Canadian and I don't really care what the plumbing is; I really don't care. I am totally indifferent to whether we have a federal or a con-federal or a sovereignty association regime, as long as the great civilizations of this country have managed to consolidate a sensible creative alliance".

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: What great nations did he call?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
The president of the commission appointed by this Prime Minister, the very Prime Minister who, day after day refuses to answer our questions on this issue in the House of Commons, is not even prepared to call himself a federalist.

The President of the Treasury Board came to the House and promised us some figures on the Spicer Commission's expenditures, but he is still Mr. See no Evil. We have hear no evil, see no evil and speak no evil. Speak no evil, Mr. Speaker, is the Prime Minister who never rises from his seat and is even afraid to answer our questions about Confederation. Even worse, Mr. Speaker, the chairman of the commission established by the Prime Minister to find a formula to save Canada is not even willing to call himself a federalist. He referred to the government's policy as "plumbing". Mr. Speaker, plumbing is one of those important things that make a house work. I would like to know whether he is prepared to live in a house without plumbing.
Mr. Speaker, I think that finding a formula for power sharing is important where Canada's revenues are concerned.

That is why I say that it is time for real change. Close to 1,500,000 Canadians will be on the unemployment lines as a result of the economic policies of this government. We have a Minister of Employment and Immigration who was just bragging about their wonderful record in the House of Commons-1,500,000 Canadians without hope.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Some record.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: One in six Canadian children goes to bed hungry every night. Bankruptcies skyrocketed last month, 55,000 last year alone.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
What a record.
Government Orders

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: When confronted with these sorts of facts, what do the Minister of Finance and the President of the Treasury Board do? They slash and cut. They slash $100 million from the Canadian Jobs Strategy. If that Minister of Employment had any concern for the people she is supposed to be representing, she would have done the honourable thing and resigned after her Minister of Finance gutted the proposals for the Canadian Jobs Strategy.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
They slashed almost a billion dollars from programs to help Canada's poor and increased unemployment insurance premiums for the salaried people of this country by a whopping 24 per cent.

Mr. Speaker, in his budget, the Minister of Finance announced that he was going to cut $525 million in funding for non-profit organizations over the next five years. In 1991-92, $75 million will be cut. In the Estimates tabled last Thursday by the President of the Treasury Board, it is impossible to find out which organizations will be affected. R. B. Bennett gave us the dirty thirties. This Minister of Finance is giving Canadians the nasty nineties. Worst of all, it is clear that the minister and his cabinet are no longer content with merely putting medicare in intensive care. The budget makes it clear that this government wants to kill off our once proud health care system. The minister's cutbacks will reduce transfers to the provinces by $338 million next year and over the next five years provinces will have to make do with $2.3 billion less,

March 5, 1991

specifically in relation to the minister's budget. These cuts signal the end of medicare and our post-secondary education system, which is also put in grave jeopardy.
In the estimates alone, the minister's own figures tell the tale of over a billion dollar cut this year alone in the insured health services program.

On page 19-8 of the Estimates, we see a cut of over $1 billion in the Insured Health Services Program. Altogether, Mr. Speaker, this means $2.3 billion worth of cutbacks in transfer payments, in addition to a total of nearly $5 billion representing cutbacks in health services, education, subsidized housing and welfare services. This Budget and this government have launched a premeditated attack on the weakest members of our society.
We find that this billion dollar cut which is part of a $2.3 billion cut specifically in relation to transfer payments and a total of $5 billion in social spending is a direct attack on those people in our society who cannot afford to help themselves
Is the Minister of Finance telling the senior citizen who is waiting to get into a hospital bed that she is going to have to pay the price?
In 1985 this minister was forced to back off a vicious attack on senior citizens' pensions. He was forced to back off when a rather sprightly woman by the name of Mme Solange Denis got her way into Parliament and confronted the Prime Minister with those telling words: "Good-bye, Charlie Brown". Well, Mr. Speaker, it is about time we tell the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance that Canadians are going to say to those who would viciously destroy our medicare system: "Goodbye, Charlie Brown".
Not only has our medicare system long been the envy of the world, it is ironic, cruelly ironic, that at a time when the United States is moving ever closer to the establishment of a national health care system, our own government, this minister, and his cabinet colleagues are pushing us, kicking and screaming, toward an American health care system. For the sick, for the elderly, for the
disabled, health care is often the difference between life and death.
What does the minister have to say to those Canadians who depend on our health care system? What does he say in his budget? I quote:
I recognize that limiting the growth of transfers under Established
Programs Financing raises concerns about the ability of the federal
government to continue enforcing national medicare principles under
the Canada Health Act.

They are the words of the Minister of Finance who states in his own budget that national medicare principles may no longer be enforceable under the Canada Health Act. He recognizes that Canadians are concerned, but he will not do anything about it.
Thatcherism may be dead and buried in Great Britain, thank God, but it is clear that Margaret Thatcher is alive and well, and living in Canada, and she is writing the Minister of Finance's speeches.
The EPF program was established in 1982 to replace existing federal funding arrangements. We recognize that EPF is not working as well as it should. Our leader, the hon. member for Beausejour, has made this point again, again and again. Many provinces have been diverting EPF transfers into general revenue funds. We need to ensure that federal dollars transferred for education and health are spent on education and health. Restricting Canada Assistance Plan benefits is not the answer. The poor living in Edmonton, Vancouver, Montreal or Chicoutimi are every bit as deserving as the poor in Winnipeg or Halifax.
Liberals believe the way to improve the system is to ensure that money diverted for health and for education is spent for health and education. Liberals also believe that the national government has a national responsibility to continue funding health care and education so that Canadians can have a guarantee of national standards from coast to coast to coast.
Tories believe the best way to help the system is by cutting off funds for medicare and students. Liberals believe the way to save the system is to spend the money where it is most needed. Why are the minister and his government turning their backs on the sick, the elderly, the disabled and Canada's youth? I will tell you why, Mr. Speaker. They do not give a damn about the sick and the
March 5, 1991

elderly because they, their Prime Minister, their Minister of Finance, and the rest of their tired government are not listening to Canadians. In January and February of this year, while the government was busily dismantling anything that makes us unique as Canadians, members of the Liberal caucus were crossing the country listening to what Canadians have to say. Thirty-five hearings were conducted with more than 300 submissions. We heard from business associations, labour unions, working men and women, social action groups, municipal and provincial representatives, cultural organizations, and ordinary Canadians.
Liberals listened to what Canadians had to say, and what they had to say is this. This government has lost the trust and confidence of the Canadian people. The economic policies of this government are hurting single mothers, children, students, workers, small businesses, and the shut-ins and sick.

Continental economic restructuring is taking place at the expense

With this budget, and with these estimates, the ministers are merely passing the buck to the provinces. Mr. Speaker, Canada is a country built by the will of its citizens, both men and women. It is a complicated country; characterized by its great diversity, it extends over a vast geography, its people speak several languages, including two official ones, and live within cultural communities scattered over many regions.
This very diversity is our strength because it allows for the expression of an open society. But it is also its weakness, because its unity is difficult to maintain. Canadian men and women have succeeded in building a great country by sharing common values, by establishing such common institutions as Medicare, by setting up a unifying infrastructure, a country with its own distinctive voice on this continent.
However, ever since they came to power in 1984, Mr. Speaker, the Tories have made every effort to destroy what unites us as Canadians.
In his very first budget, the Minister of Finance was already striking at the root of our common values. Who does not remember the battle fought in this House by our colleague, the late Jean-Claude Malepart, who, together with Mrs. Solange Denis, forced the government to back down in its attack against the least affluent people in our society. The values expressed here by the former member for Laurier-Sainte-Marie are those which hold us all together as Canadians, such values as universal access to medicare which this government is in the process of trying to jeopardize.
The minister, in 1985, withdrew his proposals under the pressure of public opinion. Now, Mr. Speaker, the minister will have to withdraw as he did in 1985, failing which he would implement his program to destroy Canada in a sneaky way.
Over the years following 1984-85, the government dismantled VIA Rail, the main physical link holding together eastern and western Canada. The government silenced Canada's distinctive voice on this continent by developing its international policy on the model of Presidents Reagan and Bush. As far as our foreign policy is concerned, Canada is no longer an independent state, for it upholds the line set in Washington. This has been another devastation since 1984.
The government has committed our country to a Free Trade Agreement which is currently threatening our social programs, including our unemployment insurance plan. The government has sold out our interests to foreign investors without any control. It has weakened the vitality of our culture by denying Radio-Canada and the CBC the resources they need.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the Tories do not understand how important it is for the CBC to maintain its presence everywhere in Canada. Perhaps they do not understand the very specific role regional stations have played in holding Canada together from sea to sea.
As members of the Liberal Party, we certainly do. We are ready not only to speak out, but to support financially, morally and spiritually the institutions which keep this country together, for without them, we would be faced with economic and constitutional chaos due to this government's policy.
To mend matters following the failure of the Meech Lake Accord the Conservative government has set up the citizen's forum chaired by Mr. Keith Spicer for the purpose supposedly of consulting Canadian men and women. We learn now that this is a blank cheque which was given to Mr. Spicer and the members of his great committee who are not even willing to state that they are federalists.

speechtext:
A bathtub without a stopper, as my colleague the hon. member for Saint-Denis puts it.
Just when we and all other Canadians desperately need realistic new solutions, just when we need rational

discussions, and just when we need to regain confidence in our national institutions, the Prime Minister and his creation are deceiving us once again.
When will the Prime Minister stop his amateurish game of playing Russian roulette with the future of our country?

The Prime Minister, as usual, is rolling the dice with the lives of Canadians as he has done so many times before. This time he is rolling the dice with the president of a commission who refuses even to state that he is a federalist. Just when Canadians desperately need realistic new solutions, just when they need rational discussions, just when they need to regain confidence in their institutions, the Prime Minister and his creation are deceiving them once more.
When will the Prime Minister stop his amateurish game of playing Russian roulette with the future of our country? When will he bring forward real constitutional reform that will give Canadians hope and belief once again in a federal and a national system that many of us want to protect, cherish and build upon?

This government, by shamelessly abusing the privileges of democracy, is responsible for the fact that Canadians have lost all confidence in our political institutions. This government, by deliberately engineering a recession, has pushed millions of our fellow citizens closer to poverty. This government's economic policies have undermined our industrial base and destroyed the source of our collective wealth. And now, Mr. Speaker, it is going after one of the jewels which is the pride of Canadians in Montreal, Vancouver and Halifax-our universal health insurance program.
Let us not kid ourselves, Mr. Speaker: by gradually withdrawing from this program funding the central government will lose our capacity to set national standards for medicare.

The transfer payment cuts have wielded a vicious attack on our capacity to have a health care system which is portable, which is universally accessible, and which gives Canadians good health care whether they live in Montreal, in Vancouver, in Hamilton, or in St. John's.
Government Orders

The government reduces health care funds, slashes appropriations for education, and cuts back financial support for the environment. It may be a bizarre and ridiculous coincidence but the amount taken out of the environmental budget is exactly the same as projected defence expenditures after March 31. Everybody knows the war is over but it so happens that the government has set $600 million aside-the very amount taken from environment-claiming the money will be for war costs after March 31.
These cut-backs can only create a larger long-term deficit, a social and environmental deficit. Mr. Speaker, health, education, and environment are our assets for the future. Funds earmarked for them are investments. They are not losses, as the government sees them, they are investments.
Mr. Speaker, the deficit is a fact which confronts millions of Canadians day in and day out. One million children live below the poverty level. One and a half million Canadians are out of work. In our supposedly developed country, 25 per cent of our fellow Canadians live in poverty. That is Canada's real deficit.
The Minister of Finance justifies his budget on the basis of personal forecasts; if they prove to be accurate, he says, the country will be just fine. How are we to believe the Minister of Finance when he assures us that inflation will be down to 2 per cent next year and that the deficit will be reduced to $6.1 billion in 1995-96? How can we believe members opposite when they talk about the figures of the Conservative government?
This same Minister of Finance predicted in 1985 that this year's deficit would amount to $18 billion. Mr. Speaker, we Liberals did not double the debt over the past six years. That was done by this government. We did not say in 1985-during a mandate of the Conservative government-that this year's deficit would be $18 billion, the Minister of Finance did. His predictions have ended in failure, just where he is now headed as he is confronted with the aspirations of Canadians. Are we expected to believe the government, remembering as we do the day they told us that administering the GST would cost $325 million, yet we found out in the Estimates tabled this week that about $700 million will be more like it, including salaries?

Government Orders
How can we believe the predictions of this government which a mere three months ago predicted that the administration of the GST would cost us $325 million. We learned, again hidden behind the pages of chaos of the minister, that in fact the GST administration alone is going to cost Canadians more than double the original prediction. It is going to cost them $700 million; two-thirds of $1 billion, the cost for collecting.
Canadians and Liberals have been calling loud and long for a new economic plan. We want a plan based on lower interest rates and a lower dollar. We want adjustment programs.
I think we should cast ourselves back to the promise by this Prime Minister who, upon introducing the free trade agreement, guaranteed that there would be specific programs for those workers who lost their jobs as a result of the free trade displacement.
What has he produced? Not one single program to help those 1.5 million Canadians who he is predicting will be on the unemployment lines next year, and not a single program for those hundreds of thousands of people in my city, in my province, in the manufacturing heartland, in the province of Quebec and across the country who have lost their jobs as a direct result of his government's trade deal.
The Minister of National Revenue could not even convince his own brother to stay in Canada. He is moving his company down to the United States to take advantage of the marvellous deal that this government signed away with Americans. He promised the programs but he never delivered.
We have been calling for policies which would help Canada restructure and modernize its work place, and retrain its most precious resource: its workers. Liberals have been calling for a government that will not only base its policies on survival of the fittest, but rather on the survival of all Canadians, concern for the sick, for the elderly and for our young people.
We on this side want to see policies which create jobs, which bring back economic growth, and which will end the Conservative government's destruction of our competitiveness and industrial base.
Last week we heard one of the persons who is oft-quoted by the Minister of Finance, Jeffrey Simpson, say in a column that John A. Macdonald would not recognize this Conservative government's agenda, because John A. Macdonald believed that the government had to have an agenda for people, and that this government's agenda was made in one department and one department only: the Ministry of Finance. In fact, it has been on the backs of those who should be defending the poor and the defenceless.
One does not have to be a political scientist to realize that the last six years have been a race for the survival of the fittest, and that this government is run by Darwinians who believe that those of us who cannot help ourselves can take a back seat and see our medicare system destroyed, our social welfare benefits cut and our unemployment insurance pulled out from underneath us.
It has given us a made-in-Canada recession which the Prime Minister himself has admitted the government induced. It has given us record high levels of inflation vis-a-vis the inflation in the United States, and specifically the spread which is important to those who are looking at long-term small business investment. Now it has rendered a death sentence on medicare. Post-secondary education is already in jeopardy.
Canadians are fed up with the heartless policies of this government. They do not want the GST. They do not want cutbacks to medicare and post-secondary education. They do not want the gutting of VIA Rail. They do not want rural post offices to be shut down. They do not want local television programming eliminated by the CBC. They do not want rural newspapers to have their line of communication cut off specifically as a result of the policies of this minister and this government.
Canadians want our Canada back again. We want back the institutions which helped create us, which shape us, which make us different from our neighbours to the south. We want back the programs that protected our sick and our elderly. We want medicare. We want post-secondary education and we want a government with a heart.
Canadians want this government to go and they want it to go now. They want real change.
March 5, 1991

This budget is not a financial statement. It is a political indictment of six and a half years of a government that is killing Canada piece by piece by piece by piece. It is tearing us apart limb by limb, and now it is going to take the heart out of us, the heart of medicare. This budget by the Minister of Finance and these estimates are the last straw. It shows the true face of this government and this cabinet.
We are now looking across the floor at the mothers and fathers of de-Confederation, as my colleague the hon. member for Windsor West called it. The Canadian people find this government and this finance minister guilty: guilty of killing VIA Rail, guilty of killing CBC, guilty of killing post offices in rural areas, guilty of killing medicare, and now guilty of killing off the very capacity of Canada to survive as a nation.
The verdict is clear. It is time for real change and, if the Prime Minister had any real courage, he would call an election and put the question to the people.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak on Bill C-97, which is asking for the House to approve funding for the deficit, but I want to remind the House and Canadians who are watching that of course what the government is asking for today is another cheque to fund its failed economic policies, because it is this government that has increased the debt to this nation by twice as much since it came into power in 1984.
I listened with great care last week to the budget speech of the Minister of Finance and I, like all Canadians, looked for some new ideas, some innovative thinking, a new plan to get Canadians back working and to get Canadians out of what is now a deepening recession. Sadly I did not see this.
I think it is important to remind ourselves that a budget is not just simply an economic tool, but a budget also defines the priorities of a government. It defines the kind of political ideology the government has. It also defines whose side the government is on. Clearly this budget is not on the side of working Canadians, of middle class and low income Canadians. There is only one side for this government and it is the corporate side, and all the rest of Canadians are forgotten and left out of this budget.

Rather than fighting this recession, this budget simply reinforces it. Rather than creating greater equality in our country, this government is widening the gap between the regions and between the rich and the poor. speechtext:
Canadians deserve a government that can build this country. Sadly, this budget like those before it has simply shown, once again, that this government has no new ideas, it has no agenda to get Canada moving, to get Canada working. While words like "competitiveness" are used, what is actually done in this budget makes Canada less competitive, less able to move into the 21st century, and less able to compete in the world economy.
A budget, any budget, of course, is always predicated on the predictions and assumptions about what will happen within the economic sphere. But I want to remind this House that if we look at the government's economic record of last year and its predictions, and the inaccuracy of the predictions that were made in previous budgets as we approached this year's forecasts, we all must have a very healthy skepticism.
I want to just remind this House that last year the finance minister predicted that inflation would fall. Instead, in January, primarily related to the goods and services tax, the inflation rate was at an unprecedented 6.8 per cent, the highest since the Liberal recession of the 1980s.
The finance minister last year predicted that we would have a deficit of about $28.5 billion; instead it will be over $30 billion. Last year he predicted that short-term interest rates for 1990 would be slightly over 11 per cent; in fact they were 13 per cent and higher. And he predicted that growth would rebound strongly in 1990.
Well, the unemployed do not need to read this budget. The children in the lines of food banks do not need to read this budget. They know the reality, they know it every day.

March 5, 1991
Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, the current recession brings back painful memories of the recession the Liberals brought about in the early 1980s. We are now faced with record numbers of banckruptcies and farming businesses being garnished, a 10 percent rate of unemployment, a growing gap between the rich and the rest of the Canadian people as well as people queuing up at food banks and soup kitchens.
All this government managed to do, as the Liberals did, was to maintain high interest rates and impose wage controls coupled with cuts in social programs. Why are we in a recession, Mr. Speaker?
The Minister of Finance suggested it was because Canadians have been living beyond their means. Try and tell that to the mothers waiting in line at the soup kitchens or unable to go and look for a job for lack of day care.

The finance minister says our wage demands have been excessive. Tell that to the construction worker, to the nurse, to the cook, to the bank teller, to the government worker and to the millions of Canadian families who have less money in their pockets each year this government is in power.
It is the first generation where it appears that our children will have less of an opportunity to improve their economic circumstance than we did as young people. Something is very, very wrong.
This government seems intent on blaming the victim: It is the workers' fault, it is the unemployed's fault, it is the poor's fault. But let us set the record straight. Let us put an end to the myths perpetuated by this government. We are not in a recession because of Canadian families; we are not in a recession because of Canadian workers or senior citizens; we are in a recession because of a high interest rate, an over-valued dollar, the goods and services tax, the Canada-U.S. trade deal and the destruction of national programs. That is what has brought on this recession.
This has been called a made-in-Canada recession. That suggests that Canadians from coast to coast helped to make it. I want to say that this is a made-in-Ottawa recession. It is a recession made in the office of the finance minister and that is the place it should be dealt with.
The budget presented last week represents the government's response to this recession. The finance minister announced proudly that he would stay the course. Well that is a little bit like saying, as the canoe heads towards the falls, the person who is paddling the canoe says: "We are going to stay the course." Despite the reality, it is clearly an illusion of expectation over reality. So what does the steady course mean for Canadians? Well, it means more cuts to health care and post-secondary education.
In the supplementary estimates tabled this morning at 11 o'clock, we saw that $728 million less will be available in health care as we learned in the budget last week. So, in fact, it is not a $1.1 billion cut to transfers to provinces for health care, it is $1.8 billion.
Just today at 11 o'clock we learned in the Supplementary estimates that for post-secondary education there will be $301.8 million less for the training of our young people. However, at the same time we see the government's priorities; the government is going to spend $154 million more to administer the collection of the goods and services tax. Somehow this government seems to want to just keep repeating the same old mistakes.
Today a report was released about the $1.1 million spent last year to send out a flyer to tell Canadians about the goods and services tax. All the Prime Minister had to do was talk to the Canadian people about what they thought about the goods and services tax. But, no, this government wanted to spend $1.1 million to tell every Canadian what every Canadian already knew: that this tax was a regressive tax, an inflationary tax and an unfair tax for all Canadians.
The government says it is going to stay the course. Stay the course on the GST, stay the course on cutting health and education, social housing, job training, cuts to culture and cuts to the environment.
The finance minister asks Canadians for patience. A senior citizen who has worked all of his life, a veteran who has fought for this country and has the right to spend his final years with dignity and respect, every day sees the results of what is happening in this country.
How shocking it was for many of us to see the headline last year in one of Canada's major newspapers of 700 senior citizens standing in line at a food bank at 7.30 in the morning, waiting for it to open. This is the future we have given our senior citizens. Surely, young people must
March 5, 1991

be asking today what their future is to be as this government stays the course.
A child who has only seen substandard housing, who only knows want and poverty, cannot wait ten years for things to get better. In fact, he or she cannot even wait for interest rates to come down. We are letting a generation of young people know only want, when many others in our society can live very well. Surely our responsibility as a country and the responsibility of a government is to say yes, we want a strong economy, a strong business community. That is important. As well, a government's role is to take care of those people who, for whatever circumstance, do not have a reasonable standard of living.
The finance minister asks for more restraint. But we already see many people in an economic straitjacket. He asks for more sacrifices, but who is asked to make the sacrifices? Well, to begin with, it is middle income Canadians. Two-income families will be paying out almost $400 more now for their unemployment insurance alone.
The increasing of those premiums also affects the small business community and the community which provides the majority of jobs in Canada. The small business community is the heart and soul of many of our communities, particularly smaller communities throughout Canada. Small businesses, many of them family run, and all families, are being hit for the first time with the goods and services tax that is costing them hundreds of extra dollars a year.
This government cannot say there are no more taxes in this budget-well, perhaps not specifically in this budget, but the economic policies out of which this budget flows clearly have made it less and less possible for average Canadian working families to own a house, to simply make ends meet from week to week.
Who else is the finance minister asking to make sacrifices? Clearly the sick-I have already noted the cutbacks to health care; to students; to the poor, to the homeless, we have cut back social housing once again by 15 per cent-to the unemployed.
I remind the House, Mr. Speaker, that during the time of the trade debates this government said that it would implement its adjustment program for workers, particu-

larly for older workers. I have been from coast to coast in this country, and virtually nowhere is this program in place in any real way to meet that promise.
The government said that public sector workers will make sacrifices, that the provinces, the territories, and of course the municipalities will make sacrifices. But from that list-and it is a long one-there is one group that is not mentioned at all or asked to make a sacrifice, and that is the corporate sector. It is the corporate sector that is making a profit. Once again, we see that not one tax loophole has been closed, that there is not one new corporate measure to address those profit-making corporations who now still do not pay one cent in taxes. Nothing. Silence.
What about the tax loopholes such as the interest deductibility that corporations have, the business entertainment tax deduction, the $100,000 capital gains exemption, tax breaks for real estate developers? Why does the government not seriously look at bringing back some balance in the tax system by imposing a minimum corporate tax for profit-making companies? We know it used to be that individuals and corporations paid roughly the same amount in income tax, and now it is the individual taxpayer who carries by far the largest share of the burden.
If this government were really serious about sharing the burden, it would be reflected in this budget. It would close those tax loopholes. It would say that everyone was going to pay their fair share and that it is time that the rich and the powerful paid their fair share.

Well, you do not have to go very far from Bay Street these days to see the real tragedy of the increasing gap between the rich and the poor, and two blocks from Bay Street you can see Canadians-young men, young women, older men, older women-sleeping in the streets. Millions of Canadians know the real thing; friends, neighbours, and family members looking for work.
It seems in this budget there is an implication that maybe Canadians do not want to work. But those of us who have worked in this field, who have worked in this area, know the devastation to the human mind and the human soul of not being wanted by your society, of in fact being rejected by your society. Day after day as you look for a job, you hear the same answer, the same response. You cope with feelings of worthlessness; you try to meet rent payments, mortgage payments, try to put meals on the table.
The effect of unemployment goes far beyond economic hardship. An unemployed person is not just another statistic. Every one of us in the community is affected when our neighbours, our families, are suffering from unemployment. It is not just the problem of the individual who is unemployed. All of the statistics indicate that unemployment contributes to a higher rate of family break-up, a higher rate of family violence, of substance abuse, and other social crises. There is a real human cost. There is a real human deficit.
Perhaps 1.5 million unemployed Canadians is acceptable to the Conservative government, but I say that it is not acceptable to the New Democratic Party-

It is not acceptable to Canadians.
The finance minister would have us believe that there are no alternatives. He has no margin in which to manoeuvre. He has no choice but to pursue policies that would punish Canadians.
I want to challenge that view because the government is not powerless. There are choices, there are different ways to do things. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, a budget is not just an economic tool, it is a reflection of the ideology of a government and a political party.
Instead of giving the Senate $5.6 million-but, no, it is not $5.6 million, after the supplementary estimates it is now $8 million-instead of giving $8 million more to the Senate, instead of investing in a relic of the past, why not invest in the youth and their future.

speechtext:
Instead of giving $24 million more to CSIS to spy on Canadians, why not invest in aboriginal language programs and cultural programs. Listen to Canadians. There are choices; tough choices it is true, but on the one hand you have Canada's spy agency, CSIS, getting $24 million more, and you have other programs, human services, that are being cut.
I mentioned earlier that the government has now cut about $1.8 billion from medicare. It could have cut out the business lunch tax deduction and saved Canada $1 billion. That is a choice. So there are choices. Instead of cutting medicare, cut business lunches. That is where the priorities lie. It is shameful that this government has chosen to turn its back on those Canadians who are the most affected by this recession and to take the choice against those Canadians and not for the future.
If this government is interested, as it professes, in economic growth and international competitiveness and in reducing the deficit, it should be lowering interest rates, lowering the dollar and introducing fair taxes.
March 5, 1991

Government Orders
We know that bankruptcies have increased tremendously in the last year, but again, bankruptcies are not just a statistic. They are that small business down the street that no longer is operating, that family that has worked so hard to build something because they believed in their community, and their country that has been destroyed by one economic policy of this government, keep the interest rates high. What it has done is it has kept the bankruptcies high too, and that is not good enough for Canadians.
Any budget, any economic policy, should surely look to investing, not just in today, but in the future. Every analyst that looks at the Canadian economy makes two points, virtually without exception, that we are a country which no longer can simply live off our natural resources; that we must in order to be competitive globally develop our research and development so that we can be ahead of the game in that area. We must ensure that we have a skilled work force, a well trained work force, if we are in fact to have a modem economy to develop the kind of leadership in technology that we know Canadians can do, because it has been done by Canadians in the past. That means investing in education, not cutting education; investing in research and development, not cutting research and development; and investing in job training, not cutting out jobs.
This is not idle rhetoric. This is simply a fact. If we want to have a modem country, if we want to move forward, we must have a highly skilled work force and we must get people working. We hear a lot about productivity statistics in Canada, but what about the loss of productivity of a person who is not working? That is one of the greatest drains on our economy because after all, people who are working can pay taxes, can contribute their fair share and can assist in getting this country back on its feet.

A few weeks ago, the Prime Minister said in Toronto he had no intention of dismantling Canada. This is the same Prime Minister who privatized 20 Crown corporations, destroyed VIA Rail, eliminated rural post offices, destroyed communications programs for native people, dismantled the CBC and, in last week's budget, continued his attack on national social programs, especially health insurance.

Why this contradiction, Mr. Speaker, between saying two weeks before that this is a Prime Minister that stands for a united Canada, that the Prime Minister does not want to dismantle Canada. On the other hand, we see the facts that speak for themselves. I think the reason is simply that the Conservative vision of Canada is nothing more than a vision of Canada as a marketplace. The government's only role is to help the private sector flourish. If that requires that some people are poor, that some regions are poor, if that means the destruction of national programs based on fairness and equality, well that is just the way it has to be, in the political ideology of this government.
Canada has been more than that. It has not been that Conservative vision that really is just simply a corporate vision, and it is not the New Democratic Party's vision. We see a Canada with national values, with national institutions that reflect those values, and national goals that go beyond economic growth that include justice, equality and humanity. We see a federal government that works in the interest of all Canadians, a government that says, through its programs, through its financial planning, that we care about those Canadians from coast to coast to coast who cannot find a job, who need to have a better standard of housing and a better standard of living.
The New Democrats say that Canada is not just a collection of 26 million producers and consumers, we are people bound by history, by friendship, by values, and bound by the wish for a better future for our children.
The national health care system is a good example of what that is about, because it is about providing health care for our citizens, yes, but it is about equality. It says if you live in an outport in Newfoundland, in a community in the eastern Arctic, on the west coast, in central Canada, as a Canadian, we want to ensure that health care is a responsibility of the government to provide. It is not what you can afford, it is something that we will provide as a government, as a country because it is part of what makes us a country.
We say that whatever income you are entitled to or you have, you are still entitled to that kind of health care, to an education. Surely Canadians should at least feel that as a Canadian they will be able to have adequate shelter, but in many major cities this is not a reality and many of

Government Orders
those people who do not have any shelter, the homeless, are children.
These are the kinds of quality achievements, of our national health care system, that we point to with pride. In fact, that other countries look to us and appreciate the kind of political decision it took to implement such a program.
So, when the government systematically continues to undermine and destroy the medicare system in this country, it not only threatens the poor in all regions of this country, it threatens an achievement that unites our country.
The same thing can be said about development assistance. We recognize in this country that whether you are in the maritime region, in the north, central Canada, or the west, we, as a people together, have a responsibility for each other. That is a value that unites us. It is a value that is the hallmark of the kind of compassion that, as a country, we have been able to express and, so sadly, is being quickly eroded by the corporate agenda of this government.
It defines the kind of responsibility that each individual has, but also it is what we have together that defines us as Canadians and, indeed, as world citizens.
I want to just mention that in this budget the government has not only made it far more difficult for those in this country, the middle and the lower income people, but it has found almost a billion dollars to fight a war in the Persian Gulf, and once again cut development assistance by $1.6 billion. Can we really continue in 1991 to believe that if we want to see security in the world, if we want to see peace in the world, we must assume our responsibility and ensure that people throughout the world have their basic needs of food and shelter met. We have a responsibility to do that.
It seems that we can always find money to fight a war.
If there is to be any change as we move to the 21st century, there must be money to feed people, both here and abroad.
If we are to have a strong and united Canada we need to have a government that gives us reason to be proud, that gives us something to believe in, and that gives us achievements to share. We must have a government and an economic policy that gives hope to those who are presently suffering. How can we talk about national unity if there are hundreds of thousands of Canadians who feel they have no hope?
Right now, in cities like Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver there are tens of thousands of homeless. There are poor neighbourhoods where the birth weight of newborn babies is lower than in some parts of Latin America. Fifty per cent of aboriginal children in this country live in poverty. Throughout this country, there are 3.3 million Canadians living in poverty.
There is no hope for these Canadians in this budget. Surely the hallmark of our nation, of any nation, should be the ability to feed, to house, to educate and care for each and every one of our citizens.
To those who would suggest it is naive to think that we can afford to do that, I say it is naive to think that we cannot afford to, and continue to call ourselves a civilized society. To those who say that social cuts, greater inequalities, a less caring society are requirements for international growth and international competitiveness, I suggest they look at the eight strongest economies in the world. If you look at that, what you will see is that the gap between the rich and the poor is the highest in the United States. Canada comes about fourth out of eight countries. It is the lowest-that is the gap between the rich and the poor-in Japan. Japan is a country we often cite as being a successful economy.
We might do well in our society, when we talk about the economy and analyse economic policies, to remember that that gap between the rich and the poor represents how successful an economic policy has been. This economy in Canada fails that test. If we are looking at how successful economic policies have been, look at the absolutely incredible increase in food banks and shelters for the homeless. The economic policies of this government have failed on that count.
It is time to destroy the myths. You can have growth and equity. You can be caring and competitive. There is a different way. There are choices. There are alternatives
March 5, 1991

This government has simply not shown the political will to take them.
Finally, I want to say that I hope Canadians will see that we are only as strong as each of us is strong. There is tremendous work being done in this country by volunteers, by those who work in the community, by those associations that often work at a much lesser wage than other organizations, just simply to make the community better.
One of the things I find veiy distressing in this budget is the proposed cuts of grants to organizations, some $75 million. They are not named, but what that means is silencing the voices, as it did last year. In last year's budget it was silencing the voices of aboriginal people and of women. It was cutting out the essential services in our community that are provided by those people who do it out of compassion and out of caring.
If through cutting back on those organizations that provide much of the infrastructure in our country, that this government says it wants to see everyone share the burden, well, I would suggest to this government that it can make real choices, that there are real alternatives and that if it cares about the Canadian people and indeed if it cares about the future of Canada, the choices that are reflected in this budget and the estimates that have gone after it, and the Supplementary Estimates, must be changed. They must be changed now.
We need a government that stands for national unity, that says: "We care about equality for all Canadians and we are going to pursue that". If this government cannot do it, then I suggest it step down and allow the Canadian people to make a decision.

Mr. Speaker, I have just gone through a pretty tough hour.
I listened to the hon. member for Hamilton East and to the hon. member for Yukon. Both would have had Canadians believe that Canada does not have a debt problem and both took the view that what this country needs is to spend more and more.
What they set before this House and before Canadians was a long list of programs that they would advocate ought to grow and expand. Thken in isolation, viewed as
Government Orders
programs in and out of their own merit, in many cases most Canadians and most members of the government would not disagree that those are programs of merit.
Totally lacking and utterly failing in the analysis is the question of affordability and what cost will go back to the Canadian taxpayer.
For every dollar that a Canadian today sends to Ottawa in the way of taxes, almost 40 cents goes to pay for the interest on our accumulated debt. Yet in spite of this debt that grows because the debt was there, there is a calling from the Liberals and the NDP for more spending, more growth, more ideas, and more creation of new programs and expansion of old ones without any single consideration for the utter chaos that this nation would ultimately end up in if we do not bring its debt situation under control.
Take a look at the debt of the federal government, and then add on that the debt of 10 provinces added together, the debt of all of the municipalities of Canada, and the debt of private persons across the country for mortgages for homes, businesses, cars, Visa and MasterCard.
Coupled with that is the recognition that what debt is is having today for a commitment to pay tomorrow. Those two opposition parties that express so much concern for education, the youth, the children, the sick, the poor and the elderly have, in effect, said: "Let's have today and to heck with the next generation."
That I believe Canadians everywhere will reject as an inappropriate policy that would put Canada into the same position as many Latin American countries and that would sink us in terms of a nation that is unable and unaffordable because they have talked about the capacity to add program upon program without consideration for the fact that we are in a debt situation.

subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION
THE CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the legislation recognizing the equality of the two official language communities in New Brunswick must be entrenched in the Canadian Constitution. This is how the rights of the Acadians of New Brunswick will be best guaranteed. Otherwise, they will be vulnerable to any political change either in Canada or in the Atlantic provinces.
In the present circumstances, it is essential that the rights of the Acadians be recognized formally by entrenching Bill 88 in our Constitution.
In this time of uncertainty, when we expect dramatic and radical changes to change the face of our country forever, the entrenchment of Bill 88 would be a positive gesture toward the most dynamic francophone minority in Canada: the Acadian community of New Brunswick.
The day when Canada will be redefined is drawing nearer and nearer, Mr. Speaker, and unless the constitutional guaranties essential to the survival of Acadia are in place, it could mark the beginning of the end for us.

subtopic: THE BUDGET
THE BUDGET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this Conservative government claims its budget will cut the deficit. This will reduce interest rates and thereby get economic activity moving ahead again.
This is the exact strategy followed by Margaret Thatcher in Britain. Thatcher and her Conservatives cut back the public sector and raised taxes heavily on average people in Britain.
The result did eliminate the deficit. They reached a budget surplus of over 25 billion pounds in the last three years, but instead of interest rates going down, they went up to 13.5 per cent in February. Inflation went up too, to an average rate of 9 per cent as of January, so the connection our government assumes between no deficit and lower interest rates just does not exist.
It has taken the British 11 hard years to learn that Margaret Thatcher was wrong. I hope it will take Canadians far less time to see that this government is wrong too.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
IMMIGRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in communities all across the country, there are Canadians waiting for their spouses to be reunited with them. Their spouses are in countries all around the world and are caught in a web of bureaucracy and inefficiency. In not just a few, but in thousands of cases husband and wife have been separated by one or even two years, waiting for immigration authorities to approve their applications.
This government has paid lip service to the objective of family reunification but, in practice, the system is inefficient and bogged down.

I call on the minister, in the name of compassion, to ensure immediately that applications to unite husband and wife are accelerated. Families are at stake. Now is the time for action, not words.

THE BUDGET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget introduced on Tuesday, February 26, has been called among other things heartless by the opposition, and yet the business community feels that we have not gone far enough in cutting government spending, although it does support the major thrust of the budget.

COMMUNICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Emperor Marcel Masse arrives as Minister of Communications with great expectations and new clothes. With his new office furniture and renovations costing in excess of $100,000, he devised great communications schemes.

THE BUDGET

Mr. Speaker, the measures contained in the Minister of Finance's budget will make it possible for Canada to leave recession behind and start on the way to economic growth.
In addition to reducing the deficit, the budget will contribute to a reduction of interest rates and a renewal of confidence, two essential ingredients to economic recovery.

subtopic: VICTORIA CROSS

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
subtopic: VICTORIA CROSS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently the Monarchist League of Canada and others have discovered that when the Government of Canada, two decades ago, decided to Canadianize awards, honours, and decorations it also made Canadians ineligible for British awards and honours, thus excluding Canadians from awards for which they had been eligible for centuries.
With the outbreak of the war in the gulf which, thank goodness, has apparently ended without Canadian casualties, the attention of some focused on awards for valour in battle that could be won by Canadians and discovered that the legendary and prestigious Victoria Cross no longer was among those available to Canadians, as Canadians. Indeed, it has been gone for nearly 20 years, but they did not notice.
Now we are told that a proposal is before cabinet to establish a new cross of Canada to replace the Victoria Cross. This change, we are told, is part of the evolution of Canada as a nation. But surely so also is the VC a part of Canada's history and Canada's heritage, and not just the heritage of Canadians of British ancestral origin. For example, the first Nova Scotian to win the VC traced his origins to Africa, for he was a black man called William Hall.
Why not establish a Canadian award that respects and recognizes our history and heritage? Why not the Victoria Cross of Canada?
