Mr. Speaker, when I concluded at one o'clock, prior to lunch, I had just undergone two speeches in this House, which in the name of lowering interest rates gave a litany of things they would like to spend money on. I want to summarize that part of my comments very quickly and then move on to another subject.
Surely every Canadian everywhere has to ask the question: If the debt is to grow without end, is health care more secure? Is education more likely? Is housing more probable? Is job training more certain? Surely, the more the provinces, the municipalities, the federal government and citizens themselves extend what we have today into tomorrow by borrowing and borrowing so that some future generation has to pay, clearly the weaker becomes our social safety net; not stronger but weaker.
While the aspirations of those of the Liberal and the NDP are laudable aspirations to be commended and congratulated, surely they must come face to face at some point with the reality that we cannot just wish for these aspects of life; we have to earn our way to be able to afford them.
I believe that a former member of this House, who represented a Toronto riding and then became the leader of the New Democratic Party for the province of Ontario, is going right through that exercise at this very moment. He went into an election campaign for the province of Ontario, promising that there would be no increase in university tuition fees. He went through an election campaign in which he said that he would offer, as was revealed today in Question Period, 20,000 new housing units.
March 5, 1991

The only reason he is changing his mind is not because these aspects of life have become negative. It is because the new premier of Ontario came face to face with reality. He came face to face with the recognition that we cannot just wish for things, but rather have to put in place the building blocks that will allow the economy to be able to afford.
What separates the government party from those of the two opposition parties? It is not the recognition of what might be good for citizens. It really comes down to the simple difference that what the NDP in particular would like us to do is to wish for a greater redistribution of wealth, without ever putting in place at all any capacity for the creation of wealth. If we cannot create wealth in this nation, we cannot have the aspirations satisfied that so many citizens want.
I would like for a few moments to turn to a very different subject-one that showed up in the budgetdealing with the use of tobacco and the taxes that apply to it, and to give my reflections on why I believe the government has approached this issue in the right way.
The use of tobacco in this country, in all countries, in every country, among every person of every age group, is something that brings harm to our health, that costs us in lost time on the job and that costs us severely in terms of our medical costs. It is the only product on the Canadian market today that is harmful to a person's health when used according to the manufacturer's intentions. It is a product for which there is no safe level of use. Many people point to other products and say these are also harmful. Those other products usually are harmful if abused, but for the tobacco product there is no safe level of use.
Therefore, I think it was appropriate when the Minister of Finance was drawing up a budget that he would add three cents tax per cigarette.
I want to extract from that what else he might have done that he did not do. Because of the involvement of Canadians in defending freedom in the gulf region, because of the involvement of Canadians to ensure that the citizens of Kuwait would be able to retain and to have their homeland, this budget was one that had to find enough capacity to pay for that expense.
It would have been possible for a six cent per litre increase in gasoline to raise the same amount of revenue
Government Orders
without increasing income tax. Clearly such a move would have been inflationary and it would have hit hard on trains, boats and airplanes: all modes of transportation. In a country like Canada, so large in its geography, such an impact would have been very serious.
We could have raised the same amount of money, had we added a two-cent per cigarette tax and a two-cent per litre tax on gasoline. But what is important is that a one-cent tax on cigarettes is equal to two cents of tax on a litre of gasoline, in terms of its net to the Government of Canada, and that even includes the projections for those Canadians who will quit smoking as a result of the higher price.
One approach would have been inflationary, whereas the other one has an impact on a habit that is harmful, that is damaging, and that is threatening to the health of Canadians everywhere.
When we take a look at what is happening in our country in terms of tobacco use, one observation that can be made is this: very few Canadians older than 22 or 23 years of age begin to smoke. If they have got to that point in their life without smoking, in all probability they will remain non-smokers for the rest of their lives.
What happens from the early twenties throughout the rest of one's life is that education is increasingly having an impact on the smoking habit. However, between approximately 10 years of age and 17, 18 or 19 years of age, but particularly in the early teen years, price is very much related to whether or not young people will start the habit of smoking.
To put a tax of three cents per cigarette on manufactured tobacco products and tobacco has a very positive impact on keeping young people from smoking.
I think it is very much a case that we have to put in place the kinds of policies which tend to decrease the amount of use of tobacco in this country for all of the harmful reasons we all know are there in terms of health costs.
This can be said of a tobacco company: A tobacco company is nobody's friend and it is everybody's enemy. After making that comment, I also want to take a moment to say that I recognize and I am fully aware and very cognizant of the fact that there are persons who make their living from the tobacco industry. In particu-

March 5, 1991
Government Orders
lar, I address my comments to those producers who grow tobacco and make their money from that product.
While it is the case we are in a society that is becoming increasingly more sensitized to good health and good environment, one cannot debate this issue and not have compassion for and even bear the obligation of having to go further to put in place the kinds of research that will seek out alternative crops, to seek out alternative opportunities and to put in place safety nets, because these persons are now having their incomes jeopardized for reasons not of their own causing.
While on the one hand I am very strongly committed that the more we can do to reduce tobacco use in this country, the better off our whole nation will be. We are able to generate tax revenues for our country without inflationary pressures. At the same time we bear a burden to those who earn their income from such ways where they need other options in order to maintain good family life on what is good agricultural lands and they need to have some kind of protection.
The dangers of tobacco are not confined to direct users of cigarettes. While 35,000 Canadians every year, year after year, each year will die from the use of tobacco, an additional 3,500 die from side-stream smoke or from being in the environment of heavy smoking. Persons who work in certain bars or in certain confined areas where smoking is a heavy, habitual habit, just by their presence in those rooms are obtaining lung diseases and heart diseases that are causing them to suffer the pangs of what happens from the tobacco industry, which has grown on the basis of providing poor health for citizens everywhere.
What I find sinister about the tobacco industry is that prior to the 1940s and 1950s the major users of tobacco were males. Somewhere about that time we were becoming as a North American society more cognizant of good physical fitness. Men throughout North America began to reduce tobacco consumption, and advertising was put in place to direct and to influence more females to take on the use of tobacco. The product Virginia Slims and the insulting slogan of "You've come a long way, baby" were used in advertisement to try to attract women to the habit of smoking.
As that stabilized, what then became the next market of the tobacco industry was to focus on young people, up until such time as governments put in place the restrictions on advertising that disallowed not only the use of tight jeans and the kind of lifestyle advertising that made young people think that smoking was a chic thing to do, but banned it altogether so it was not even an influence within the Canadian market at all.
What the tobacco industry is doing today by going into the Third World nations, selling high tar tobacco, not even processed or refined to what we think of as an acceptable standard in North America, and trying to perpetuate the use of tobacco among these relatively uninformed, unsuspecting Third World citizens is a fact of business policy that simply cannot be tolerated or accepted.
They somehow need to diversify and get out of their industry not only for the sake of the health of Canadians, not only for the sake of the fact that they have been involved in a product that is morally wrong because it kills so many people. They have also to bear a burden that they as a company, not just government, owe something to the farmers who produce their product and that they as major tobacco companies need to get involved in the rediversification and the ability of these producers to be able to raise new products without having to have their livelihoods stripped away.
This product, which is as addictive as cocaine and heroin and has been established and researched in some 50 nations by more than 3,000 creditable studies has been proven time in and time out to be harmful to one's health, dangerous to those who are in the presence of smokers. It is highly addictive. It is causing one of the major costs of our society in terms of lost time and health damage. I think the time has come when clearly we as Canadians everywhere have to send the signal that the habit of smoking is unacceptable. It is intolerable but, most of all, we should commend those in the budget process who used that process to stop at least another
10,000	to 15,000 young people from developing the habit.
Hopefully next year there will be another increase in the tax on tobacco. I hope the companies will bear a major burden in helping provincial governments and the federal government to re-establish new possibilities for those in the tobacco growing regions, because they bear the burden of doing something humanitarian rather than

simply going from men, to women, to children, to the Third World, perpetually trying to sell a product that should not be on the market in the first place.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, generally the member who made the speech takes the opportunity to respond to a question or comment. This was not done in this case.
I think it is not just a question of getting into a bidding war as to who could demonstrate the sincerity of their opposition to the evils of tobacco by the severity of the tax, whether it be three cents a cigarette or fifteen cents a cigarette. I think that the hon. member who spoke for the government is undoubtedly sincere in his concern about the effects of smoking and about the extent to which nicotine addiction is every bit as strong as that of cocaine or heroin.
On the other hand, although I do not oppose the tax in the budget, no one has every suggested that the solution to heroin addiction is to up the price of heroin, or to up the price of cocaine, because many of these problems are much more deep rooted than simply the price of the particular product. I would caution the hon. member against any sort of simplistic correlation between price and the ability to break oneself of the habit. In fact, if anything, trying to solve these problems through taxation tends to punish poorer addicts over wealthy addicts. If you are one of those people who unfortunately cannot break the habit of smoking, if you happen to be affluent, you are going to continue to pay the price. If you are poor and you cannot pay that price, but you must continue to pay it because you cannot find your way out
Government Orders
of the addiction, then other things are going to suffer-it might be the kids, it might be other things.
I would certainly encourage the government, if it is serious about trying to break Canadians of nicotine addiction to look not only to the tax system, but to look for other ways to help people shake what admittedly is a very difficult habit to break completely and utterly, as I know from my own experience and from the experience of so many other people.

Yes, and I could appreciate why you would want that distinction.
What the hon. member raises is certainly a legitimate question. Why are we treating cocaine and heroin differently from tobacco? The answer, I think, is fairly straightforward and it is that we have gone through several generations where tobacco was, and is today, legal.
If tobacco use were discovered today, if Sir Walter Raleigh popped up today and said: "Guess what I have found, this stuff that you can chew, put in your nose, and smoke in paper," and if we knew the research that we know today about it, I virtually would guarantee that this product would be illegal. Its addiction is equal to that of heroin and cocaine, and its health hazards are such that no matter how you use it, it is harmful, even being in its presence.
But cocaine and heroin came on the scene when we knew their damage and they were illegal and they are illegal at the present time.
Then the hon. member says: "Well, what about this question of price?" I thought I had answered that in my formal comments. Persons above the age of 20 who have not yet smoked do not develop the habit. With very rare exception they do not develop the habit. What research has established is that in those years from age 10 through to the end of the teens, the single most impacting factor to decrease tobacco use is price.

March 5, 1991

We could make it illegal, but then we come face to face with the question of what purpose would it be to make a product illegal with a portion of our society so strongly addicted. They would find it virtually impossible to quit. They would perform all kinds of inappropriate social behaviour to try and put in place the continuation of a habit to satisfy an addiction.
By implication, though, I think that that inference might have been made. The hon. member for Winnipeg Transcona says that he did not intend that, and I take him at his word.
I think that price has been established to be effective in keeping young people from smoking. When we look at the other options that a government might have had for raising the funds-very clearly one it might have gone to is a tax on fuel-there would have been an inflationary impact. I think this is a commendable way to go to raise funds without being inflationary and, at the same time, put a real, significant damper on a bad habit around the world wherever it may be used.

Mr. Speaker, I also want, in the context of the budget, to suggest to the member that the government is willing to consider punitive taxes in order to eradicate bad habits, which is what we have here in the form of the tobacco tax and the argument being made by the hon. member. I wish it would have considered suggestions made by members of my party and members of the environmental community, about looking at what we might call "green taxes" or "eco taxes" or "environmental taxes", that is, taxes which would discourage the use of products which are harmful, not just to the individual environment of a smoker's lungs, but to the global or shared environment of the planet earth.
There was a lot of talk, for instance, about a carbon tax. In the same way that smoke pollutes the human body, the greenhouse effect and various other things which go into the atmosphere are having a long-term deleterious effect on the global environment. It seems to me that at some point governments are going to have to come to the view that they ought to use the tax system, among other things, because I would go back to my other argument that the tax system itself is not the only way to deal with this, but to see the tax system as one weapon in the arsenal, so to speak-forgive the military analogies- that the government has to deal with environmental
problems. Therefore, you could look to taxes which would discourage the use of certain kinds of products.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to stand in the House today to discuss with members Bill C-97, which will borrow in excess of $26 billion and which members know is part of the government's budget.

What I intend to do is to ask four questions. First, what are this budget and this bill doing for the economy, the economic development of Canada and this government-made recession we have in Canada? Second, what will this budget and this bill do for national unity? Will they make things better or worse? Third, how will this Budget affect education? I raised that question in this House last Wednesday. Finally, once those facts are established, I would like to ask a last question: how much hope and confidence should we, Canadians, put in this government, based on the decisions made in this budget and this bill?
March 5, 1991

Members know we are working within an ideological framework that goes something like this. There is a high dollar, high interest approach to economic development. Basically what is supposed to happen is that inflation should be controlled. Supposedly that should fuel the economy and create jobs.
We need to admit-and I believe this is quite true- that what we have received this year is not terribly different from what was presented in previous years. It may vary somewhat in degree, but for all intents and purposes it is extremely similar. What have been the government's successes to date? Let us review those quickly.
Many members will recall the victims of the government's policies. I am referring to VIA Rail, with 2,700 Canadians no longer working. I am referring to CN, where there has been an announcement to the effect that 2,900 Canadians will lose their jobs. I am referring to the Air Canada privatization, where another 2,900 Canadians are without jobs, many of them extremely skilled people. There are pilots who have devoted much of their lives to gaining the skills required, and many others in a number of other professions.
Some members will recall the Route Canada fiasco where this company was sold and where 1,900 Canadians paid and continue to pay because some of them have not received wages or pension benefits or severance benefits. I could go on.
What about the CBC cuts? This year alone they are over 1,100. Last year there were 500-odd. These are the kinds of situations in which Canadians have been placed. They are the victims of this made-in-Canada recession, of these government decisions, including this latest budget.
What else has occurred? We have been told and it has been documented that bankruptcies are at a record high. The poor in this country, which is a relatively rich one, total nearly five million, most of whom are women and over one million of whom are children. In Canada this year almost two million people will go to food banks. I am informed that perhaps as many as 40 per cent will be children and that is roughly 500,000 people per month.
Government Orders
There are in this country today five million to seven million functionally illiterate Canadians, which costs the Canadian economy in excess of $10 billion. There are over 1.3 million unemployed, and that could be going up to 1.5 million. There have been cutbacks to health, to education, to social assistance programs, to regions, to various groups-some have been mentioned today-and 33 tax increases including the goods and services tax.
What happens as a result of all of this? Quite apart from the difficulties that Canadians are suffering, the ones I have mentioned and many, many others, well, the deficit is in excess of $30 billion, $30.5 billion. And the debt will be over $400 billion.
I know that my colleagues across the way love to say that is the Liberals' fault. But I have from the Minister of Finance a signed document which says that at the end of fiscal year 1984, the debt was $168 billion. When the interest rates from that day up until now are factored in one finds, interestingly enough, that the debt should have been much less than what it is today. So it really does not add up.
We have to look at that within the global context because do hon. members know what revenues were in 1984? They were around $70 billion. Do you know what they are going to be at the end of the fiscal year? They will be almost $130 billion. That is very close to twice as much. That is a pretty good increase in revenue. So the question is, what has happened to your money and to mine?
Mr. Speaker, there has been little success. The model that is being used by the government is based on a number of assumptions and those assumptions are false. They are not working. Not deliberately so. It just so happens that the model is not operating appropriately.
Let's look at some of those assumptions. The interest rate was predicted to be 11 per cent in 1990-91. But we all know that it averaged 13 per cent. Inflation was predicted to be, I think, in the neighbourhood of 4 per cent, or a little lower. Of course, that is not so; the most recent figure of 6.8 per cent really throws the figures out. The deficit was predicted to be $28.5 billion this year; as I mentioned, it will be $30.5 billion. As you know, in 1985 the same Minister of Finance predicted that the deficit

March 5, 1991
Government Orders
would be $18 billion. That is a far cry from the $30.5 billion that it is.
What about taxes? Personal income taxes were supposed to increase by 9 per cent. But lo and behold, your taxes and mine happened to increase by 15 per cent. What about corporate taxes? They were supposed to decrease by 2 per cent. But what happened? Lo and behold, they were reduced by 10 per cent. And the 1988 corporate tax rate of 34 per cent is now down to 28 per cent.
Economic growth was predicted to be 1.3 per cent in 1990. Well, it is going to be a little more than one-half of that, .8 per cent, apparently. And for 1991 the prediction was 3 per cent in growth, and we expect the economy to shrink by 1 per cent this year.
What were the predictions for employment? It was predicted for 1990-91 that there would be 1.2 per cent growth. But what has really happened is that it will shrink by roughly 1.5 per cent.
Perhaps they have done better with unemployment. The prediction for 1991 was 8.5 per cent unemployment, and now we expect it to be, according to the most recent budget, 10 per cent, or perhaps even slightly more.
With all due respect to the finance minister, his forecasts cannot be trusted and, I hasten to add, not because he is deliberately trying to be misleading but I think simply because he is unable to predict accurately what is happening in this country, and to deal with it appropriately.
The second question that I want to address is: What does this budget and Bill C-97 do for national unity? You know, I know, we all know that the institutions which bind this country together are being systematically destroyed one by one. I have mentioned the CBC, the CBC that spoke to the nation from one coast to the other; and VIA Rail, where we could travel at an affordable price; what about the privatization of Air Canada? What about the cuts to health, education, and social assistance programs? I could go on and identify even more reductions to programs that held this nation together, that gave it a sense of purpose, that gave it direction. But they are being dismantled, and they are being dismantled in such a way that people are losing faith in government. They are losing faith in government, and they are starting to believe that this country can no longer stay together.
This budget has been defined as a separatist dream and a federalist nightmare. Why is that? We know that the federal government has been unable to respond in a sensible and sensitive way to the needs of the regions, to the needs of the people in the provinces and in the territories. What is happening is that gradually, bit by bit, they feel as if they are being blocked out. They feel as if they do not matter any more. They feel that it does not matter what they say or do; they do not count. And when that happens, the country suffers and national unity suffers.
A federal government, it seems to me and to many colleagues, ought to be able to ensure that the essential services, such as health, education, social assistance, transportation, and communications are in fact available to all Canadians, no matter where they come from, no matter what their status in life. It should be there. That is our main and most essential purpose. And that is where this government has failed miserably.
It is unfortunate because, as I mentioned before, Canadians throughout the land are feeling as if it is not working together. The great fear that I have, and that many other Canadians have, is that once you start thinking that way, it may become a fait accompli.

My third question regards education. What impact does this budget have on education? The government made more cuts in this field. After promising there would be no changes, in 1986, it brought in a 2 per cent cut. Again in 1989-1990, it cut a further 1 per cent. In 1990-1991, it imposed a freeze. Now, it has extended the freeze. The figures involved here are astronomical.
Between 1986 and 1995, the health and education enveloppes will have shrunk by approximately $33 billion. So, there will be about a third less money for education, that is to say $11 billion. That is a lot of money, an enormous amount of money!
What was done in terms of training and retraining? Where are the outstanding programs we were promised? In previous years, the amounts allocated were more or less the same without taking inflation into account though. This year, there is a $100 million cut. What was done in terms of student assistance? Nothing. While the

eligibility criteria were not changed since 1984 in spite of the fact that the cost of living increased tremendously, nothing was done.
For litteracy, $4.50 a year is granted for each of the five to seven million Canadians who need help. You cannot even buy a hamburger and a glass of milk for that price nowadays. As for research and development, a ceiling was put on that too, as you know. Research and development are most important to ensure that we remain at the leading edge of things on the economic, technological, social, cultural, and political front. So, what do we do? We set a ceiling.
What does all this lead to? As you no doubt are aware, the student debt is skyrocketing. I have here-I could quote, but I think my colleagues will take my word for it-information to the effect that it increased quite substantially over the past ten years. This means that there are more students today who, on a scale from $0 to $5,000, $5,000 to $10,000, $10,000 to $15,000 and $15,000 to $20,000, are getting $15,000 to $20,000 deeper into debt every year than there were in the past. So, what do they do? They are afraid, they quit school, and fewer and fewer of them will get a post-secondary education. We will be the big loosers.
On admission fees, did you know, Mr. Speaker, that they increased by 300 per cent in some provinces and by 200 per cent in others? One hundred per cent increases are not uncommon for admission fees. What will that do? I can assure you that if we add up the 2 per cent ceiling on student job creation, the impending closure of employment centers in colleges and universities, the impact of the GST and the 3 per cent administrative fee added on to student loans, it is no wonder that Canadian students feel crushed. This at a stage of this country's development when we are realizing that our most important resource is the Canadian men and women, educated men and women who are truly committed to the economic, social and cultural development of the country.

I have a quote here, and it is a bit embarrassing because it says: "Conservative revolution takes big leap forward." It shows that while the government continues to talk about the need for competitiveness on the world
Government Orders
markets and globalization, it ceaselessly strangles the nation's colleges and universities. We are all people who believe in the importance of education, but we must go beyond believing in its importance. We need to ensure that it has the support that it requires to do the job that needs to be done.
Let me just quote a few passages very quickly about the importance of education:
Education is about far more than the exercise of federal spending powers; it goes to the heart of the factors that bind Canada together as a country. In a country as vast and diverse as ours nationhood is often a tenuous proposition. What better place to start nation building than in our schools, our universities and colleges, and educational programs which take place outside of our institutions.
The challenges that face Canada are very real and immediate. We must begin to equip our nation with the human resources it needs to confront economic globalization and domestic economic restructuring-
Increasingly, major industrialized countries are recognizing the importance of improving labour productivity through training as a means of ensuring competitiveness.
This is from the Ontario Report of the Premier's Council Industrial Policy Studies, volume III, 1986. I could go on. The Canada Royal Commission on the Arts, Letters, and Sciences stated:
The universities also serve the national cause in so many ways, direct and indirect, that theirs must regarded as the finest of contributions to national strength and unity.

Mr. Speaker, there are several other quotes, but I must launch upon the last point now.

What kind of trust, what kind of confidence can we have in government as a result of this analysis that I have done? We know that the promises have not been kept and I would not be nearly as upset as I am if they had returned and told us why. But they kept on going without even the simple courtesy of explaining.
I pointed out that the assumptions of inflation, interest rates, et cetera, are wrong, absolutely wrong. What upsets me is the minister last week would not admit that he had cut health and education, and he has almost-$1 billion, and half a billion in education. When is a cut a cut? We know that the government's policies have had very, very little success, that the revenues increased from $70 billion to $130 billion with a deficit that is in excess of $30 billion, a debt that will go over $400 billion. Yet it

Government Orders
continues: the unemployed almost $1.5 billion; the food banks, almost 2 million people will go there this year.
We know that there has been unfair taxation where the poor get poorer and the middle class is getting hammered and hammered and they are becoming poor.
I am pleased that my party has put a task force on taxation together and they it will look at progressive taxation. It will look at proposals from my colleague, the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood, as well as Professor Brooks from the University of Toronto. It wants to ensure that this country's taxation is as sensitive and sensible as it could be.
This budget has attacked the regions and its people. The government was wrong in 1984-85. It was wrong in 1985-86, 1987-88, 1989-90 and it is wrong this year as well. The Minister of Finance wants us to believe him. We really tried. We found that we could not. We cannot and we will not.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened closely to the clearly expressed views of my colleague the hon. member for St. Boniface, and I commend him for that. Still in his remarks he raised a number of issues which have me wondering. I know he is an expert in the education field and that he held senior positions in his province. Elowever, Mr. Speaker, I was surprised a few times when the hon. member for St. Boniface referred to the money spent on education throughout Canada and told us that in a few weeks or months we will be witnessing the complete collapse of our national education system in the ten provinces and the two territories.
Sure enough, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian government can no longer afford to invest as much money as we would like in education, research and development. But most people know that money does not solve everything. Back home, in my city of Shawinigan, we have a general and vocational college which this year has the best budget ever. But in concrete terms, for instance, last weekend the local newspapers reported that 70 per cent of the students at the Shawinigan CEGEP cannot pass a quality elementary test in French. Yet the government spends a fortune on that institution of learning.
Unless I am mistaken, Mr. Speaker, the member for St. Boniface is convinced that we will solve our problems by spending more money for education and more money for the health care system in Canada. I do not share his views. I would suggest that the provinces have a significant role to play when it comes to allocating the funds they have for educational purposes.
If we examine what is going on in Quebec-and I imagine it is the same thing in other provinces-we see that, owing to labour agreements, a physical education teacher will teach mathematics next year and religion or ethics four years down the road before returning to physical education, without the benefit of a refresher course. We have reason to believe that a lot of money has been spent, but because of a major flaw in the collective agreements between the province and the teachers, it would seem that all that money has been badly expended.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like other hon. members, I rise to take part in the debate on the borrowing bill, Bill C-97, which of course goes to the heart of the recent budget and goes to the heart of the present economic problems that are being faced by this country.
I listened with some interest to both the recent debates that have taken place and the discussions that have occurred over the past several weeks. It strikes me that only occasionally do people speak to what surely are the essential issues in the matters that are presently before us.
Surely we are addressing the economic health of the country and the degree to which the federal government, in the way that it can control the expenditures and revenues of the country, can contribute to the improvement of that economic health.
As we think about matters related to the debt and the deficit, I think there is a danger of looking only at the narrow economic issues, whether it is the regular growth of the debt, which is in many ways overwhelming, if not suffocating, or looking at the annual deficit charges which are still enormous. In fact, if one looks at the amount that will have to be paid on the interest alone on the debt that currently exists, it is such a monumental
figure of some $43 billion that it almost overwhelms almost the totality of all our annual social expenditures.
This is not an easy issue to resolve. If it was, we would certainly not be debating it here and we would not have had a succession of budgets and economic measures seeking to contain it.
I would like to begin by looking beyond the immediate problems that affect the debt and the deficit. Those of high interest rates, high dollar, perhaps less than adequate productivity, threatening inflation and, of course, at the moment veiy large and unacceptably high unemployment. I want to look at the context of the country itself and what we are faced with.
In Question Period today and in many Question Periods, there was debate about how we are resolving our constitutional difficulties. Again, the danger is that we look at these in the context of the kind of legalisms or to extend it a bit, the packages of rights and privileges that extend to various jurisdictions: the provinces, the federal jurisdiction, or beyond the provinces to the municipalities.
It would be important for just a moment to think about the totality of all of this, of the very country of which we are a part. It is a fascinating if not, at times, a frustrating country to understand.
I had the opportunity last year to serve on the special committee of the House of Commons, the Charest committee, which attempted to break the logjam with respect to the Meech Lake agreement. I do not want to regurgitate all of the arguments that went pro and con around that issue. But I want to look at the perceptions that affected that consideration and the perceptions that I suspect very much affect both the Spicer commission and the joint committee of the House of Commons and Senate. Here is where I think we engage ourselves in considerable difficulty.
What strikes me, as someone who has been in and out of public life now for a quarter of a century, is that there seems to be greater and greater difficulty for Canadians generally to see the country in its totality. It has become much easier, one might almost say seductive, to look at the country through a particular microscope, in a particular locality and with an almost singular set of characteristics. While it is true that each one of us makes our home in a specific community, accompanied by specific family, neighbours and friends, the sustenance of that
March 5, 1991

local community is a much larger reality. One that is even larger than Canada itself and Canada is, to say the least, uncomfortably large.
The old saw of an earlier Prime Minister, Mackenzie King, that most countries have too much history and this country has too much geography seems to be particularly true in the experiences of the last decade.
In the debate affecting the borrowing bill, a certain amount of attention has been focused, certainly from this side, about the degree to which in the final years of the Trudeau government expenditures far outran revenues, something like 30 per cent or more and there was a rapid accumulation and an augmentation of the debt.
That same period of the early 1980s also saw an attempt to resolve the national sense in the elaboration of the Constitution in 1982 and 1983.1 believe that in a sense by attempting to resolve something, that may have been much more difficult to resolve than we realized, we opened a kind of Pandora's box and created a kind of expectation, if not a desire, for people to try and satisfy and resolve all their local anxieties within some kind of new national context and not really being sure of what that might be.
Those questions are still out there. In some ways they may have been further enlarged upon or touched upon in terms of our renegotiated economic understanding at least with the United States through the free trade agreement. If there are two things that affect the character of Canada and Canadians it is our sense of what it means to be united as a country and in relationship to the United States.
All of this could be cast, and has been cast by some, as a kind of negative experience but I want to suggest here today that it also has the seeds within it of a positive opportunity. While Canada is very big and its problems for those of us who are Canadians may seem very large, the world of which we are increasingly aware is even larger, tougher, and more difficult. We only have to reflect on the experiences of the last few months and in particular the experience with the gulf crisis to realize how abundantly true that is.
I was not that closely involved with all of the detailed aspects of either the gulf crisis or the gulf war, but just before hostilities occurred in mid-January, along with colleagues from both sides of this House, I visited two countries that certainly were heavily impacted by the effect of the gulf crisis.
Government Orders
Even today as I stand here the people of the Sudan who have unfortunately been bled by a government that chose in a rash moment to support the actions of Iraq have paid a rather heavy price in terms of finding limited access to desperately needed foreign assistance at a time of a major internal famine threat and crisis.
Many of us are deeply troubled by the fact that as many as perhaps seven million to nine million people at the moment are suffering the risk of famine in a situation which far too few people know anything about but which, all too sadly I suspect, as the news and interest related to the gulf subsides they will become painfully aware.
This is only one example of the world which Canada is a part of. A few months ago I attended an international meeting concerned with matters of security, not security in the way we have traditionally thought of it in terms of military expertise and systems of national defence. This is security of a kind that raises fundamental questions about the health of the planet to survive the rapidly deteriorating situation and ecological breakdown that is occurring in hot spots of the world, such as parts of Africa, but is already showing signs of threatening even the protected parts of North America.
I see my colleague here from Saskatchewan. He could speak feelingly about the recurrence of very threatening drought in the 1980s in the province of Saskatchewan and in parts of the United States.
We have major environmental challenges. When we talk of security in the 1990s and beyond, I believe we will be spending much more time thinking about ecological security and resources in the same kind of mind set, the same kind of magnitude as countries have been prepared to devote to systems of national military defence.
These are a few examples of the world in which Canada exists, and here I want to raise a very strange problem.
When I travel with others to parts of Africa or Asia to discuss with them their particular needs, how Canadian volunteer organizations, institutions, churches, universities, labour unions, businesses and others can be helpful, there is an automatic willingness to engage in conversations with Canadians because we have a record of being helpful in a disinterested way that does not carry with it

Government Orders
a great hidden agenda of some kind of exploitation or unfair advantage.
We do hope for improved and beneficial relations, but in a way that is acceptable to both partners. I can still recall a few months ago being with a number of friends in Ethiopia discussing with them some of the acute challenges and problems that are faced by one of the poorest countries of the world, with a population twice the size of Canada.
During the conversation, as we had spent much time discussing this project or that, it suddenly turned to Canada and I was asked to give an indication of what was important that was going on in Canada.
As I began to describe some of the matters which seem to preoccupy so much of our time and attention, I saw people's eyes glaze over because they could not understand how these problems, which from their point of view seem so infinitesimally small, could so dominate our national agenda and our national attention.
There is a strange paradox or contradiction in this. I think that Canadians, our political parties and our institutions have to rediscover what are the real priorities for this country in the world of the 1990s.
A starting point has to be where we live, and that is the purpose of the bill that is before us today. That we get our own economic house in order. There can be no satisfactory health to us in any other kind of terms if the management of our own resources and economic wellbeing is not being responsibly looked after.
A great Canadian, a man who had tremendous insight into the fundamental differences between Americans and Canadians, once said: "The real difference in business terms between Americans and Canadians is that Americans like to make money and Canadians like to count it". That was Northrop Frye.
I think it says a lot about a certain sense of responsibility that we have. I believe there is a good deal of discomfort among members of all parties in the fact that we have not been as effective as we should be in restoring the economic health that we need for this country.
While I have heard a fair bit of criticism about this particular program activity, expenditure, reduction or
another, I have heard very little about how we can in a sense take the direction that the Minister of Finance, the President of the Treasury Board and others have outlined by way of suggesting a safe, sure and secure path out of the economic strangulation that exists with spending still far too much of our revenue resources to meet an unacceptably high deficit and a national debt. Surely the challenge to all of us is to work together on that proposition.
The other day I was at a meeting with the president of the Economic Council who raised a problem that I had never thought of in economic terms. She said that one of the fundamental weaknesses in the Canadian economy is that we may be too affected by an adversarial situation.
Of course it goes without saying that the parliamentary tradition that we are all a part of is based on a certain level of adversarial activities. It is the constant testing of governments that ensures that they are doing what is responsible and that also indicates that the opposition are keeping governments on their toes.
I think she was meaning more than that, that within the Canadian experience of acting responsibly in an economic sense there is a need to work together to work our way out of what I regard as an extremely dangerous and difficult situation. None of us can be happy by the fact that the deficit at $30 billion is still far higher than it should be.
I would like to challenge all members of this House, and I suppose particularly those who are in the opposition, to contribute to this debate and others in a way that would suggest how we can make further and effective reductions in that, because, ultimately, the most important thing we can do in achieving economic recovery, and with that, environmental and social recovery, is in raising the confidence level of the Canadian economy. I fundamentally believe that that will not happen unless we can prove that we are serious about getting our own economic house in order and reducing, in a significant way, the sure strangulation that the continuing debt and deficit have effected on the Canadian economy and on our people.

Mr. Speaker, I look forward to this opportunity to participate in the discussion on the borrowing bill. Let me say to my hon. colleague who has just sat down that I too remember very well-I think it was December 1984, just a few weeks before Christmas-the visit that he, as the then famine ambassador for Canada, and I, together with the member from Edmonton Southeast and Lynn McDonald took to Ethiopia. Certainly I could not agree with him more that that kind of experience will not leave any of us because it was at the height of the famine and it was early on. What we saw, in particular having seen it just before Christmas, just before coming home for that great spiritual but commercial celebration here at home, was quite a startling contrast.
I have to say to the hon. member that when I remember those scenes, when I remember those people, nothing in my experience has ever affected me as much or for so long a period of time, then I become one of those representing one of Canada's poorest provinces, Newfoundland, one of the highest areas of unemployment in Canada in the riding now named Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte when its name changed, I become one of those who has no hesitation defending even in times of restraint Canada's foreign aid spending development assistance.
I know I speak with absolute assurance on behalf of the people of my riding, that even though they live in the poorest province in one of the poorest constituencies of the 295 in Canada, the people of my constituency would not want to see the books balanced on the backs of the very poorest of the poor in the world. I hope the government will bear that in mind and will not feel some political obligation to make cuts.
I hope that if we are involved, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs has said, in the reconstruction of Kuwait and Iraq that those funds will not be diverted from existing aid programs, that we will not deny those who live in the sub-Sahara so we can do reconstruction in Kuwait or Iraq. That too would not be proper.

I want to say a few words about this government's spending program and its request for borrowings and the budget. The reality of a borrowing bill and the reality of a budget is that it is far more than just an economic statement. A budget is far more than an economic blueprint for the government. It is far more than a ledger of assets versus liabilities. As well, a budget is and must be a political statement. The budget reflects, after all, the priorities, the problems but also the potential of a nation. A budget is the reflection of the choices that a government makes in determining its spending program. Ultimately, a budget tells us something about the values of a society.
I have no hesitation in saying that I have a great many problems, a profound disagreement with this borrowing bill and this budget. It is not a disagreement founded on how much is raised and how much is spent. It is not a fundamental disagreement with the notion of practising a measure of frugality. It is not a disagreement with the Minister of Finance's seven year old objective of getting the deficit under control. He has been telling us every year since 1984 that that is his primary objective. However, the national debt has more than doubled in those seven years and the deficit has not been reduced by very much. So I do not disagree with those objectives, although they have been missed. No. My objection to the borrowing bill and to the budget is the kind of vision it paints of this country.
The member who spoke before me talked about values. I know that member is genuine when he talks about values. I know he feels things very deeply. I have never asked him directly, but I sense this. If you spend time with someone in a place like Ethiopia, a form of osmosis begins to happen. You begin to take the measure of people. I know that when it comes to values, the perception of the continued meltdown as is assuredly going to happen as forecast in the budget, the assured meltdown of medicare in this country; the assured meltdown in the ability of Canadian youth to have access to post-secondary education in this country, that evolution, as is foreshadowed by this budget, causes members of vision, I would suspect, a great deal of trouble.
If Canada is allowed to continue with the kind of spending program, the kind of priorities as outlined by the Minister of Finance, we are not going to recognize
Government Orders
this country in a very short period of time. We are not talking about 30 years, or 20 or 15 or even 10 years from now. We are talking about three or four years from now.
Do Canadians realize that this budget puts in place cuts for health, education and social assistance to the tune of $5 billion over the next five years and that within five years we are going to have as many as four of the ten provinces getting no transfers from Ottawa for health care. What does it mean when four of ten provinces get no transfers from Ottawa for health care because of these cutbacks? It means we can no longer talk about a national standard of medicare in Canada, because the national government cannot dictate a national standard if it has not put its money where its mouth is.
What does that mean? It means if you come from Ontario, which has some fiscal capability and there is a cut in health dollars, the provincial government makes up the difference and hopefully, you maintain the quality of the health care. But if you come from Newfoundland, where there has been a cut in federal dollars, and the provincial government has no ability to make up the difference, then health care goes down.
It means we are building a Canadian society where the notion of being a Canadian used to mean that in some fundamental ways, we are all equal whether we come from P.E.I. or Rosedale, or Newfoundland or British Columbia. We used to be equal in terms of our health care across this country. We all knew that if we got sick, God forbid anything else that went wrong, we would be looked after. We used to know that if we were totally down and out and had no other means, at least under the Canada Assistance Program we would be looked after. We always knew that if we were unemployed, we had our unemployment insurance. We knew that in our retirement, we could retire with the dignity of a Canada pension. All of these things, health care, access to quality education, unemployment insurance, and I suspect in the minds of people my age we are wondering whether there will be at this rate an old age pension, the security of an old age pension cheque.
All of those things are not about dollars and sense. They are reflections of the values of a nation. Do we as a nation value the notion that whether you come from east or west, north or south, rich or poor, you are entitled to quality health care? Is that not a Canadian value? Can it

March 5, 1991
Government Orders
be traded away against the bottom line of a budget estimate? Do we not in this nation believe that the brains of this country, the youth of this country, whether they are born north or south, east or west, rich or poor, Catholic, Protestant, Jew, Muslim, that every one of them ought to have an opportunity to develop the potential of their grey matter and that university ought not to be the privilege of the rich?
Mr. Speaker, every time we see another cut for post-secondary education, the post-secondary institutions raise the tuitions, and every time they raise the tuitions the universities become more and more a place for only those who have dollars in their pockets. That says something about the common values of being a Canadian that are being traded away in this budget.
I said a moment ago that I am from Newfoundland. In this country for the last 30 years we have had another concept that is being traded away in this budget. It was the concept of regional development, not a concept or a guarantee that every region would be equal because they will never all be equal, not a guarantee that every citizen would be equal. There can never be such a guarantee.
We always strived in this country whether we were Liberal governments and traditionally Tory governments to at least provide an opportunity for equality, the chance to succeed. When you play with medicare, and when you play with access to quality education, when you play with the basic sustenance of life, you deny that opportunity for equality of opportunity.
In the budget just brought down we again see cuts in training programs. The Minister of Finance announces forecasts that unemployment, which is now 1.3 million, is going to go up to 1.5 million-one million five hundred thousand Canadians unemployed, without a job, with no income, without the dignity of a pay cheque-one and a half million, the minister's forecast.
In the next breath he says: "By the way, I am cutting $100 million from our training budget". Is investing in training, giving skills, developing skills for Canadians an expense or is that an investment? Is that money wasted and thrown away or is that building on the most primary form of raw material of the country, the primary raw resource of the country, our people?
I suggest a $100 million cut to the Canadian Jobs Strategy is not in my judgment a wise investment. It is not a wise investment and would not be perceived as such in any of the constituencies of this country, whether we are talking low unemployment areas or high unemployment areas. But that cut has been made by the Minister of Finance and we on this side have asked the Minister of Finance, we have asked the government, to reconsider that cut. These are training dollars.
In Ontario, the great province of Ontario, they are really feeling as they have never felt the negative impact of this recession. Southern Ontario is taking a vicious beating. It is being de-industrialized.
The factories are closing, the workers are being sent home, but that is not the bad news. The bad news is that the factories are not reopening. They are relocating. They have gone south.
When the government brought in free trade, the Prime Minister at one point promised the most massive adjustment program that the world had ever seen. We did not get adjustment for those factory workers. Some of them who live in southern Ontario come from my province. They are now unemployed. They are coming back home again because they lost their jobs in southern Ontario.
We did not get an adjustment program in this budget. We got a $100 million cut in training funds. This budget smacks of a set of values that fly in the face of the institutional memory of government in this nation.
They are not Liberal values, New Democratic Party values or Conservative values. They are Canadian values that have evolved since 1867. They have come from the hearts, minds and souls of Canadians who distinguish themselves from that great neighbour to the south, the United States. We do not believe it is every man, woman and child for him or herself.
This is not a dog-eat-dog society. We do believe in caring and sharing. We do believe that no matter where you live, what your circumstances are, what your income is, there are some things we have in common. We are Canadians.

This budget has been written as if the Minister of Finance expected the applause that would normally be generated in the United States of America by the brutal values that are expressed in it.
Let those who have tried to suggest that this budget is really not a big deal-this budget has no big tax increase-remember that there has been a 24 per cent increase in UI premiums. It is going to raise billions. That is a tax increase.
There has been a $5 billion cut in the transfers to the provinces and so the provinces are now going to have to do what the federal government did not have the courage to do: cut programs and raise taxes.
Let those who will spend the next few months balling up their fists in anger at their provincial governments because they have cut their post-secondary programs, because they have raised tuition fees, because they have closed hospital beds remember that the source of that misery is not in the province. It is here in Ottawa.
The Minister of Finance is not fighting the deficit. He is transferring it onto the backs of the provinces. That transfer of the deficit onto the backs of the province is going to create a Canada where we have a multi-class society. Those who reside in provinces with the financial wherewithal to make up the shortfall will have one standard. Those who come from the poorer provinces will have another degree of Canadian citizenship.
This budget turns its back on Canadian history and on every Prime Minister, starting with John A. Macdonald who built the railway not because it made sense, not because it was economically viable but because he wanted to hold a nation together. He bound it together with bonds of steel.
He understood the notion of nation-building. He understood and dreamed about what kind of country this could be. This government, in six short years, most symbolized by this pathetic budget has squandered Macdonald's dream.

Do we wish to attract capable men and women to stand for public office in this country? What are the bases upon which it is not only attractive but, on a more practical level, possible for people to seek public office?
If the only requirement is that you be rich, then it is no problem. Then it does not even matter whether they pay you or not, and it does not matter whether there is a pension plan.
But I ask: What about the mid-stream professional? Most people do not come to this place in their twenties or indeed in their thirties. Most people come to this place later on in their lives. One need only look around the room and note the sprinkling of grey hair here and there to note that most people come here either midway in their professions or indeed later on. If they come later on, then the problem which my hon. friend is trying to solve by his bill simply does not exist. However, if they come here in mid-stream, what are the sacrifices they have to make on behalf of their families?
He quite rightly points out that nobody forces us to come, but they sure urge us to. They come forward, and we want good people to stand. There are questions as to viability. For example, somebody may have been 17, 18, 19 years in their profession and in their mid-forties or late forties. Maybe they have paid for 17 or 18 years into a pension scheme, and they have to abandon that to come to Parliament and start all over again.
Are we going to attract people to come here, if in fact to come here means to throw their family's financial security on a trash heap? That is really the implication of what is being suggested, it seems to me, if we look at the majority of people who stand for public office in this country.

Private Members' Business
I do not think Parliament should be abandoned to simply the rich people. We look at the desirable aspects of MPs' pension schemes and one is tempted to say: "Boy, you fellows really have a good deal". But, then, let us look at the nature of the employment.
I served for 17 years in my profession, education, in my own province of Nova Scotia. When I came here, I had 17 years in my teacher's pension plan. Of course in order to draw a pension I have to go back and work for a few more years, and I know my hon. friends opposite will do their best to see that I have that opportunity at the next election.
But there are other elements of employment in other places, the most principal of which is security of tenure. One can reasonably anticipate, on embarking in a career, that one can stay there until retirement, until one is qualified to earn a pension. Let us face it: there is not that kind of security here, and the practical realities sometime interfere.
My hon. friend talks about the amount of money that the public pays for MPs' pensions. He then proceeds to talk about all the other things that MPs are paid. I would challenge him to name any other pension scheme in this country where the participant in the scheme pays 10 per cent. I know that in my old profession in education, six to seven per cent was the normal range of contribution that was paid.
I guess what I am saying is that I am not sure one can compare apples and oranges and then draw simplistic conclusions such as his friends in the National Citizens Coalition like to do.
What I would like to see, not only for MPs but for all Canadians, is a portable pension attached to the individual so that people do not become the captives of their employers as so often they do.
Over the years when I worked for teachers in Nova Scotia, I would have teachers come in and see me who would be burnt out, who would be tired of the profession, who would be ready for a job change, and they would say: "I have been in teaching for 21 years. I am 47 years old and I am burnt out. I want to do something else, but I cannot leave because of the pension. I am locked in for life; I have to stay here".
Why do we not look ahead in pension reform and look to the notion where every Canadian, on birth, is in effect
registered for a pension. Throughout the course of their career, whether they are employed or whether they are self-employed, as they achieve earnings they make contributions to their personal pension scheme. That leaves them in a situation where down the line they have an opportunity to make their own decisions about their own pensions. If they want to retire early, they have an option to do that. If they wish certain options with respect to how they draw their pension back, that opportunity exists. It is a system, for example, that is used in the province of Saskatchewan. The teachers in Saskatchewan have an individual purchase pension scheme.
What I am talking about here is the concept that you have a pension that is attached to you. If you choose to move from vocation to vocation, from employer to employer, you have your own pension and your pension serves your particular interests and indeed ultimately serves your particular needs. Along the way, your employers would contribute, just as they do with pension schemes now. If you are self-employed, you would have the option to increase the amount you put in. Indeed, people could put in varying amounts, although I believe there should be a minimum. Otherwise, some people would say that they do not need it and then later on in life they would find out that they did, but that they had not been very wise financial planners. Perhaps we should be looking in a more comprehensive way, not just at MP's pensions, but at the pension needs of all Canadians.
The particular bill before us does have some specific problems, and I will briefly mention them, Mr. Speaker, before allowing somebody else an opportunity to participate.
First, it deals with only one aspect of the pension scheme as it affects members of Parliament. Indeed, it seems to me that you have to look at the whole package. I would commend to my hon. friend from Edmonton Southeast, who in trying to solve this problem has brought this piece of legislation forward, that perhaps a more appropriate time to deal with MP's pensions along with others is when the President of the Treasury Board brings forward the Comprehensive Public Sector Pension Reform bill which he is going to be bringing before this House. It seems to me that that would be the appropriate context in which to examine MPs' pensions as well.
March 5, 1991

There are also technical problems with this bill, problems relating to the lack of transitional arrangements. If this is not remedied, the provisions of the bill could, for example, be applied retroactively to former members, and so on. There are some missing elements with respect to the inadequacy of definitions of such things as "part-time" and "public service".
In conclusion, I would like to say that I think pensions are an appropriate thing for members of Parliament to talk about. But I think for them just to talk about pensions that affect themselves is not really a constructive and valuable use of Parliament's time. We should be concerning ourselves with pensions as they affect all Canadians. One of the things that provides for an appropriate social safety net is a pension scheme that accommodates and looks after the needs of all Canadians. And that is what I think Parliament should devote its time to.

Mr. Speaker, if the member from Selkirk would be polite enough perhaps he would like to listen to some pearls of wisdom.
Let me state the purpose of this bill as stated by the sponsor. It is to "prevent a former member of the Senate or the House of Commons from receiving a retirement allowance while the member is employed on a full or part-time basis and is not 60 years of age". This bill, an act to amend the Members of Parliament Retirement Allowances Act, is numbered C-343.
Bill C-343 is a bill about fairness. Is it fair for politicians to raise themselves above the people they serve, ignoring the rules of the private sector, to award themselves pensions of the type that now exist?
The MP pension plan flaunts at least two principles accepted in the private sector from my way of thinking. The first is the 10-year rule. MPs need work only six years before receiving a pension. Everyone else must work 10 years at least. The second principle is waiting until one is 60 years of age before receiving pensions. The average citizens, whom we are sworn to serve, do not have another option. They must wait. MPs bypass this waiting period, accessing their pensions immediately after they lose their seat or decide to leave it.
The spouse of a member receives that member's pension after death, no matter how young or successful or otherwise wealthy that widow or widower may be.
I submit that these pensions are pensions of privilege. The Parliament pension funds collect more than twice as fast as the rate allowed for pensions in the private sector, giving former members of Parliament a much greater amount to retire on than a private citizen who has worked the same amount of time. This is something I find objectionable. There should be uniformity in the system. Our pensions should not be the pensions of privilege. What kind of example does that offer to Canadians?
Most of us were middle-class working men and women before our term here in Parliament. Before being elected in 1988,1 was a doctor in practice and a professor

March 5, 1991

in the faculty of medicine. If I were to leave politics and return to this work should I decide or the electorate decide, I feel it would be wrong for me to ask Canadians to pay me a pension-salary when I would no longer be working on their behalf. There is no reason why I should not have to wait until I am 60 at least, around the same age as most citizens before they receive their pensions.
At this time, members of Parliament are adequately paid for their services. We receive a base salary of $62,100 per year and other expense allowances. Some may argue politicians leave high-paying jobs in the private sector to work for the public. Maybe so, but those people weigh their decision carefully and set their priorities in order. It should not be the burden of the people to overly compensate these politicians or any other politicians in the years after they leave Parliament Hill.
In conclusion, this bill asks us simply to make pensions less generous than they are now, to send a clear message to Canadians that we members of Parliament genuinely recognize that our country faces serious economic problems and that we sincerely care to address them.
I support this bill to send a clear and correct signal to all our constituents and to all Canadians in the interest of fairness.

until they reach 60 years of age. After 10 years their pension is locked in and they may not withdraw it after that 10-year period, nor may they claim it until they reach 60 years of age, and I think that is appropriate.
I think of members of the armed services who might retire at, say, 50 years of age and are still obviously able to work. If they work for the federal government, it is my understanding that they are not allowed to collect that pension from National Defence as long as they are an employee of the federal government. So there seems to be a double standard here. We mentioned former leader of the New Democratic Party, Mr. Ed Broadbent who was a member of Parliament for a good many years. Mr. Speaker, we are now discussing Bill C-343 which raises the question whether a former member of Parliament may continue to receive pension payments if he has joined the ranks of the federal Public Service.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, at the present time, members of the House of Commons can receive a retirement allowance under the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act, according to which an allowance is payable upon retirement to members who have contributed to the Retiring Allowances Account for at least six years.
The amount of the allowance is based on the number of years of pensionable service. Under the existing Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act, members who have served at least six years in the House of Commons are entitled to a retirement allowance as soon as they cease to be a member, i.e. on the day they resign, the day of their decease or when they go down to defeat
March 5, 1991

in an election. The surviving spouse and children of a deceased member are entitled to receive the allowance.
Perhaps I may recall, Mr. Speaker, and I think this is very important, that during our years of service, each one of us must contribute to the Retiring Allowances Account an amount equivalent to 10 per cent of our sessional indemnity. These contributions are deducted at source on each paycheque.
Those members who have supplementary indemnities as a result of additional duties-ministers, for instance-may elect to pay a contribution equal to more than 10 per cent of this indemnity. This is an important point, because we contribute directly to our pension fund during our term of office.
Everyone knows, Mr. Speaker, that an MP's work is very demanding, both professionally and personally. Many left far more lucrative jobs to come and spend some time working on building up and improving the living conditions of Canadians. We do so by conviction, to defend the ideas which we believe in and which we feel are in the best interests of all our fellow citizens.
Mr. Speaker, we all know that members of Parliament are a long way off from job security.
It does not matter what government level an individual chooses to get involved in, he never knows when he will find himself without a job. Such is democracy and I for one can only say that I agree with the system. It is up to the people to pick their representatives under the provisions of the electoral process and in light of their priorities at the time. The principle of democracy is basic and nondebatable, as far as I am concerned, and I sincerely hope that some day all human beings will be able to live under a system where each man's and each woman's right to an opinion is respected. The principle underlying the electoral process is the very foundation of the citizen's democratic choice, and that is as it should be.
But political life does create a number of difficulties, such as separation from one's family, extremely long hours, and a heavy workload, just to mention a few. All those who are or have been active in politics know that, as do others who have been closely associated with someone in this field. Throughout our mandate we have to forget all about our personal life. Ninety five per cent of our time, thoughts and activities are centred on our
Private Members' Business
parliamentary duties, be it in our ridings or here in Ottawa.
Ours are exacting responsibilities, but seldom do we have an opportunity to talk about this kind of personal considerations which are unknown to the public at large.
Regardless of our political affiliation, all members carry a heavy burden which calls for big sacrifices. I suggest this must be said as we are debating the matter of parliamentary privileges. But that is the choice we make when we decide to enter politics, and we must live up to our responsibilities.
A moment ago I alluded to the fact that we have no job security. I have more to say about it because I think it is an important aspect of today's debate.
Indeed the enduring financial insecurity which comes with the iffy nature of our occupation is part and parcel of political life. I refer to this because it is an essential issue for all citizens, men and women alike and regardless of financial standing, if ever they should choose to run for elected office.
Given the precarious nature of our profession, we ought not to withdraw the few privileges which are attached to the position and which make it possible for any man or woman in Canada to enter the political arena. We might discourage from running some excellent prospects who already know that they would be deprived of the benefits they enjoy in their current occupation or, conversely, make it possible only for the affluent to run. We would be yielding to a financial elite who could afford the luxury of going into politics, which is certainly not what we want or wish. If they so desire, all citizens should have the opportunity to seek votes, thereby ensuring that Quebecers and Canadians continue to be represented by their peers from all walks of life.
I shall never accept for instance that a small businessman who could make a major contribution to our society be prevented from doing so, for he would have everything to lose as far as his future is concerned. Likewise, I shall never accept either that a person who is not financially secure should renounce his or her ambition of sitting in this House because he or she lacks the wherewithal in view of the insufficient salaries or retirement benefits associated with the job to represent people of the same social standing.

March 5, 1991
Private Members' Business
This would be absolutely unfair and unacceptable. Far from contributing to the progress of our society, we would cause it to lose ground by depriving ourselves of the talent of these men and women with so much to contribute to our society. While trying to increase the number of women in politics, I am afraid we would be excluding them altogether because it is a well-known fact that women are often less affluent than men. Mr. Speaker, I suggest that this is a consideration we should really ponder upon.
There is another point in the bill introduced by my honourable friend which puzzles me. Why indeed should a former member of Parliament who went on to work for the Public Service of Canada not receive this retirement allowance before turning 60 years old, when the same rule would not apply to former members working in the provincial Public Service or in the private sector?
It seems to me that to pass this bill would be a serious breach of the equal opportunities principle. I think that the members of this House should ponder on this. I wonder if it would not be against the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which guarantees, as a fundamental principle, the right to equality.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, I see that my time is up.
