Mr. Speaker, I am extremely pleased to be able to support this particular bill which will bring I believe, if it were to be enacted, a sense of fairness in the whole scheme of pensions. I am delighted to join my colleague from Nepean, my colleague from Winnipeg North and I am told that my colleague from Thunder Bay-Nipigon, as well as my colleague from Winnipeg St. James, support this bill in principle.
There is in fact a double standard. We also make our own decisions with respect to our funding, our salaries and benefits and frankly, that could be and should be questioned.
It is when government is slashing health, education and social programs that people are really getting very, very upset. We can understand that. They see this kind of cutting back and they see us with fairly lucrative salaries, benefits and pensions and they become increasingly angry.
I will give a couple of examples. I hate examples because they tend to exaggerate and suggest that they go to the whole. I want to make that point very, very clear. This is not the case. There are some people who are not nearly as well off as others because of their circumstances. For example, and I am not picking on the Minister of National Health and Welfare, but he happens to be my example. He came in rather young. If he were to retire today and if he were to live to be 75 years old, and I suspect as cranky as he can get every once in a
March 5, 1991

Private Members' Business
while he will go away beyond that, he would be paid over $5 million in pension.
Many of you will know for example that it takes us only 10 years to get 50 per cent of our salary, but it takes the other Canadians 25 years to attain 50 per cent of their salaries. Most Canadians do not like that one little bit. You know as well that our cap is 75 per cent of our salary, Mr. Speaker, while for other Canadians it is 70 per cent, and there is no happiness there.

Many of you have heard about "double-dipping" even today. I do not want to pick on anyone in particular but I have to use examples. Former cabinet minister Erik Nielsen retired a few years ago and got 75 per cent of his pension at that time, indexed since retirement until now, and $133,000 as president of the National Transportation Agency.
That is a lot of money, particularly when you think of the 5 million Canadians out there. There is a double standard, and I am not sure that we ought to be doing this all by ourselves.
What should we do? Let's consider an independent third party to address questions of salary, pensions, allowances, and other remuneration. Why not account for expenditures if it is going to make Canadians feel a lot better? With respect to future increases, looking at what is happening in the private and public sectors, there ought to be things that we are doing.
I believe that we need to do something like that. We need to look at questions of transferability of our own pensions to the private sector as opposed to having a separate one. We need to look at the possibility of continuing our own pension plans when we come here.
I could have spoken a lot longer, Mr. Speaker, but I notice that you are giving me the signal. I simply want to say that-

-yes, there is a double standard, and we should not be the ones to make decisions regarding our own salaries and benefits. I think that should be someone else's responsibility.

subtopic: LITHUANIA
LITHUANIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to pursue with the government the question that I asked with respect to Lithuania sometime ago. Of course some members will know that I asked a number of questions about the situation in Lithuania and in the other Baltic States, Latvia and Estonia, over the last little while, ever since returning from there just over a year ago where I had the opportunity to observe the elections in Lithuania which brought the Sajudis movement to power.
Since then, of course, there have been other elections in Latvia and Estonia. Democratically elected governments have come to power in those republics. There have been declarations of independence. Now, just in the most recent weeks, and indeed in recent days, we have seen a series of referendas in those three republics, beginning of course with Lithuania where they had a referendum on independence and on Sunday, March 3, in Latvia and Estonia.
I think what is significant is not just the overwhelming majority which voted for independence in Lithuania where the Lithuanians, ethnically speaking, still form 80 per cent of the population, but the significant vote which independence received in Latvia and Estonia. Both of these republics have within them large Russian ethnic populations. It seems clear at this point that it is not just the ethnic Balts but others who envision the prospect of independent Baltic republics as a positive option.
I want to say that I am as glad as I am sure many others are that the central power in the Soviet Union, that is to say President Gorbachev and the Soviet Union per se,
March 5, 1991

permitted these referenda to take place. These referenda have taken place in a thoroughly legal and constitutional way, but there was a time some weeks ago when it appeared because of the tragic actions of troops in Riga and Vilnius that there might have been a move afoot to undermine and even overthrow the democratically elected governments of these republics.
I hope I am not just being over-confident in saying that it appears that is not now the case and that these governments are continuing, as indeed they have demonstrated by being able to hold the referendas which have been held.
I think it is now incumbent upon the Soviet Union and upon President Gorbachev, given the unambiguous results of these referenda, to negotiate meaningfully and in good faith with the Baltic republics a way in which their special case, as opposed to other republics, can be recognized. When I say their special case, I mean of course the fact that they were incorporated by force into the Soviet Union as a result of the Molotov-Ribbentrop agreement or the Hitler-Stalin pact of 1938-39 and that this is a factor which has to be taken into account by Moscow when it is dealing with the Baltic republics.
Given the result of the referendas, I think it is now incumbent on Moscow, as I said before, to get serious about finding a solution to the aspirations for independence of the Baltic peoples, one that can be worked out and that is a positive alternative to both the real and implied threat of force should the Baltic republics continue to pursue the goal of independence.
It seems to me that much could be gained by Moscow, if indeed it were to allow the special case of the Baltics to be recognized and to permit the negotiation, albeit a tough negotiation, of Baltic independence.
There will be very difficult economic questions to address, given the many long years of economic integration and many future years of economic integration, I am sure. There will be security questions. There will be questions of minority rights in the Baltic republics, concerns which many non-Balts legitimately have.
There are many things to be worked out, but they can only be worked out after and when the Soviet Union finally admits that it has a problem here that cannot be
Adjournment Debate
solved by force or intimidation and that has to be dealt with by negotiations in good faith.
I call on the Canadian government to do its part, now that these referendums are over, by seeking ways to persuade-not to force or anything like that-the Soviet Union that the time has come to deal with this.
I think one of the ways that that can be done is to signal an intention on the part of the Canadian government that at every opportunity, in every appropriate international forum, the question of the Baltic states will be raised, whether it is at the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe or at the United Nations. Wherever opportunities present themselves, Canada should be in the forefront of saying to the Soviet Union in the appropriate international arenas: "Look, you guys, you have got to deal with this question. It is not just a matter of the internal affairs of the Soviet Union. It is a question which belongs in the international arena, given the former independence of these republics. We want you to negotiate with them in good faith, and we want you to respect the long-standing de jure view of the international community that these are indeed independent republics and should become so in fact as quickly as possible".

Mr. Speaker, I thank you for the opportunity to say just a few words in response to the concerns raised by my friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg Transcona.
As all members of this House know, Canada recognizes the de jure independence of the Baltic states. We have never accepted their enforced annexation. We believe that their peoples have a right to determine their own future. In fact, Canada has clearly demonstrated its uncompromising support for the Baltic states on several different occasions during the course of the past year.
The right hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Prime Minister himself have both met with past leaders of Lithuania and Latvia and in some cases with the present leadership. In all cases, during the course of those meetings, I think Canada has taken the opportunity to demonstrate its commitment to the Baltic peoples who are continuing to strive for their right of self-determination.

Adjournment Debate
In addition, the concerns of Canada and the concerns of this House have been conveyed to the appropriate Russian officials, to former Soviet Minister Shevardnadze, seeking assurance that there would not be a crackdown on the Baltic states. Unfortunately, as we all know, those assurances were not forthcoming.
In fact, we were among the first to react to the unwarranted military force used against the peoples and democratically elected governments of Lithuania and Latvia.
The Soviet Ambassador to Canada was called in on three different occasions during the month of January. Our ambassador in Moscow conveyed Canada's very strong concerns to the appropriate officials in that country. In communications with President Gorbachev on January 13, the Prime Minister of Canada expressly linked further offers of Canadian assistance to the continuation of reform.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State for External Affairs welcomed the debate which occurred in this House on January 21. I can assure you that we will continue to exert the same kind of influence and pressure on the Soviet Union in the future that we have been doing in the past.
We will also continue to work with the Baltic peoples in Canada. There is consideration at the moment in the establishment of a Baltic information centre which I think would be of some value.
In conclusion, I believe that Soviet authorities are in no doubt as to the position of Canada on this matter. In fact, a member of the Official Opposition who has just visited the region recently reported that the influence and the activities of the Canadian government are well recognized there. They are also much respected there.

subtopic: JUSTICE
JUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am compelled to pursue questions relating to the David Milgaard case.
First of all, I will state a few facts. David Milgaard is Canada's longest serving prisoner. He is serving a life term for the murder of a Saskatoon nurse, which
occurred in 1969. He says he did not commit the crime. He has denied himself parole because he will not confess to that particular murder.
Much evidence has come forward casting doubt on his conviction. He applied to have his case reopened more than two years ago, and just a few days ago the Minister of Justice said "no" to the reopening of that case.
This case has attracted the attention of a nation. It has attracted attention of people who are concerned about justice. I am sorry, though, that I cannot say the same for the justice minister.
I believe that the hallmark of her handling of this case can be summed up in one word: indifference. She has not shown interest in this case. She has not shown a deep concern.
I am also concerned that the justice department approached this case with a closed mind. There is evidence that the Department of Justice was not impartial.
Take for example a report, Mr. Speaker, in The Globe and Mail of last August 1. In that report, a senior justice official, Mr. Bill Corbett, likened people who believe in Milgaard's innocence to those who believe that Elvis Presley is alive. Tb me, this reflects a damaging bias certainly to Mr. Milgaard's case, and I do not think it promises a fair hearing.
Bias also showed up in other ways. The prosecuting attorney in the case 21 years ago, Mr. Bob Caldwell, was asked to collaborate in the investigation of the case in the last few months.
We must remember who Mr. Caldwell is. Mr. Caldwell was the man who asked for Milgaard's conviction. I ask: Would he provide evidence that would reflect poorly on himself? I doubt it. Yes, let's have Mr. Caldwell's evidence under oath. Treat him like any other witness, I say. Anything less than that is contrary to natural justice.
We also have to wonder when the Department of Justice sends an investigator accompanied by the RCMP to interview a witness who testified at the trial 20 years ago. The witness was asked to visit a police station for interrogation without benefit of counsel. This occurred after arrangements were made to hold the interview at the lawyer's office, that is the lawyer of the witness.


March 5, 1991

Was this some kind of scare tactic? I have to ask the question. Was this an example of impartial, unbiased treatment? It does not seem likely. These are questions that concern me.
The Milgaard family along with their counsel have worked long and hard to uncover new evidence. The justice minister has more or less said a few days ago that this new evidence that was uncovered really would not have made any difference at the trial, that is if the evidence had been made available at that time. In effect, she was saying that the verdict would have been the same.
The victim in this case was raped and then murdered with a paring knife. Before that murder there were similar incidents of rape enforced with a paring knife, but the jurors were never told that. Had they known about these other incidents, would their verdict have been different? It is very possible. I think the minister's indifference to that is shocking.
The minister also pointed out in her statement of some days ago that a former judge from British Columbia was retained to look at the Milgaard case. That is fine in itself, but what were the terms of reference for the learned judge. We were never told. What evidence was the learned judge given to examine? We were never told. What was the judge's opinion? We never heard his opinion. We never heard about his judgment. We only heard from the justice minister what her opinion was.
If this were not bad enough, the judge's work was done behind closed door and Milgaard's counsel was not a party to any of it. This is not intended as any reflection on the judge. I am simply commenting on the process.
Finally, we must ask whether the justice department itself is in a conflict of interest. We must remember that in a case like this the justice department is asked to investigate itself. Is that a conflict of interest? Certainly on the surface it is.
We wonder about the justice minister herself. Remember, she is both the Attorney General of Canada and the Minister of Justice of Canada. Are those conflicting roles? Perhaps, especially in a situation of this kind, and we have to ask the question if we are really concerned about justice. In closing I want to say that we cannot, in all good conscience, accept the way the hon. Minister of Justice has handled the Milgaard case. I am talking about
Adjournment Debate
her handling of the case going back to day one, that is day one when she was asked or her predecessor was asked to look at this case and possibly re-open it. We cannot, in good conscience, accept her refusal to re-open the case. There are just too many questions and justice, natural justice, demands answers to those questions.
This issue is not going to fade away. It is not going to disappear. The justice minister might want it, but I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that it will not fade away. The questions are far too serious and, besides, we must remember this: David Milgaard who has been behind bars for 21 years might be an innocent man.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: JUSTICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the section 690 procedure of the Criminal Code allows for ministerial review of cases where new evidence or information provides a reasonable basis to believe that a miscarriage of justice likely occurred when the case was before the courts. An applicant may only resort to section 690 when all judicial remedies have been exhausted.
In the Milgaard case, an impartial juiy found him guilty of murder; an impartial court of appeal dismissed his appeal; and the Supreme Court of Canada refused his application for leave to appeal in 1971. Having exhausted the judicial process, Milgaard's counsel wrote to the Minister of Justice on December 28, 1988, and applied on Milgaard's behalf for relief under section 690.
Two grounds were initially raised in the Milgaard application. To assess them properly, the department requested additional information which the applicant provided in May and August, 1989. Those grounds were investigated and a preliminary report was prepared in December, 1989.
While that report was being reviewed by senior justice officials, the applicant raised additional grounds which required investigation. First, a new suspect was introduced in February, 1990. Second, further forensic results were supplied in June, 1990. Third, additional statements from trial witnesses and others were supplied in June, 1990. Fourth, a "new witness" surfaced in July, 1990.
Each of these grounds was investigated by the Department of Justice with the aid of the RCMR Since a number of new matters were added to the initial application the department at the request of the applicant's

March 5, 1991
Adjournment Debate
counsel received counsel's oral submissions in person on October 1, 1990.
The departmental report was completed and an independent legal opinion was obtained. The report, the opinion, and the applicant's submissions were all submitted to the minister who devoted a considerable amount of time reviewing the application, the facts, and the issues before the minister rendered a decision on February 27, 1991.
The proper exercise of the serious and important responsibility conferred upon the Minister of Justice requires a thorough review because the remedy is one of last resort. Accordingly the scientific issues raised in this case were referred to specialists in those disciplines for their evaluation and the authors of those reports were interviewed.
During the investigation of all the issues in the application over 36 witnesses were interviewed by the RCMP and departmental counsel. Some were questioned under oath and their answers were transcribed. The trial and appellate court record were also examined and reviewed.
During the minister's review of the case there was a careful consideration of the facts obtained from all sources and from counsel's submissions, in determining whether a miscarriage of justice likely occurred.
The minister concluded there was no body of new evidence or information which constituted as reasonable basis for believing that a miscarriage of justice likely occurred in this case.

subtopic: HOUSING
HOUSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to discuss a matter that I raised on December 11 with the Minister of State (Housing), regarding the Quebec government's dissatisfaction with federal social housing policies.
Articles published in the press gave the impression that the province of Ontario had benefited from federal assistance for social housing, at the expense of Quebec.
Created a few years ago, the Ministry of State (Housing) has introduced a number of initiatives designed to provide more help for Canadians who need it most.
Thanks to improved and sustained federal-provincial co-operation and a joint planning process for social housing, resources are now being put to better use and are better adjusted to regional needs. Umbrella agreements have eliminated administrative overlap and guarantee continuity of the planning process. In fact, these agreements direct social housing assistance to the neediest in this country, especially those who must spend more than 30 per cent of their income on housing. About
615,000	households benefit each year.
I was delighted to hear last December that the Co-operative Housing Program will be extended. Originally set up on an experimental basis, the program has helped low-and middle-income families, senior citizens, women, native people and disabled persons to find housing. The program will therefore continue to offer housing to households on modest incomes. New criteria for future residents of co-operative housing will ensure that federal funds are paid to lower-and middle-income households that cannot afford to become homeowners.
The program also provides that half the co-operative housing units will go to the neediest. The government also helps elderly Canadians in need through its social housing program. Those who do not require direct government assistance are offered a range of housing options that enable the elderly to maintain their physical and financial independence.
Since 1988, the federal government has provided for the construction of 8,811 senior citizens homes in Canada. Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, in my own riding, since 1985, federal commitments to social housing have been very impressive. As part of the non-profit housing and rural housing programs, the federal government has helped increase investment in the riding of Drummond to the tune of $14 million.
Furthermore, under the non-profit housing program, six residences totalling 175 housing units have been built which will require an annual subsidy estimated at $717,000, to be paid for thirty-five years. The capital cost represents $25 million for the riding.

Under the rural housing program, four buildings containing a total of 40 housing units were built. This represents an annual subsidy of $207,276 for the next twenty-five years. The cost is evaluated at $5,200,000.
Two buildings erected under the federal Co-operative Housing Program will receive annual grants of the order of $51,003 over a 30-year period. These costs will amount to $1,530,000.
As well, government commitments with respect to rent supplement applicable to social housing constitute annual grants of $138,348 over the next 35 years, a total of $4,800,000.
Finally, under the provisions of the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program the federal government approved repairs in 839 housing units in the riding of Drummond, an expenditure of $4,702,649.
As to rent supplement, $138,348 in annual grants over the next 35 years will account for $4,800,000.
Mr. Speaker, the last Wilson budget has earmarked $1,000,739,690 for the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, a considerable amount.
However, despite the many commitments of the government in the social field, it would appear that the federal-provincial agreement benefits Ontario at the expense of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, I always thought that federal government funds for housing poor people should be equitably distributed.
But on the contrary the articles to which I referred indicate that Ontario residents got more than their fair share. In fact the author of the article claims that the minister is more interested in looking after the housing needs of Torontonians that those of other Canadians. Mr. Speaker, it has also been suggested that these inequities date back to a number of years. If that be so, it is not time to set things straight?
Back in 1988 in Regina the federal government, the provinces and the two territories signed an agreement which was supposed to correct the situation. Now it would seem that the agreement has failed and that Quebec continues to be penalized.
I know that before our government took office the province of Quebec had decided that federal housing funds would not be invested in major construction projects. Instead the government favoured programs
Adjournment Debate
which did not entail long-term grants. As an example, the administration at the time saw fit to spend the federal money on home and apartment repairs rather than build new social housing units.
This decision was a blessing for thousands of people living in units badly in need of major repairs to be safer and more comfortable. This program in fact was a big help to thousands of households throughout the province in both urban and rural regions. One thing for sure however is that once the work was done there was no need for long-term grants.
In Ontario and elsewhere in Canada the need for new housing was more urgent than repair work, with the result that there were more construction projects spead over a number of years and subsidized over a longer period of time.
To be honest, Mr. Speaker, I know as well that Ontario got directly involved in shared-cost programs some ten years before Quebec did.
I would like to ask-I see the minister is in the House today, so this is a good opportunity for me because I have known him as a colleague since I first came here in 1984-whether that is the reason why more federal dollars went to that province rather than to Quebec, and can the minister tell the House why Quebecers who pay their fair share of taxes do not get as many benefits as some other regions of the country?

subtopic: HOUSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for his question. It provides me with an opportunity to clarify the formula used by the government of Canada for the distribution of federal social housing funds among the provinces and territories to respond to the housing needs of Canadians across the country.

The objective of the federal government in social housing is to help low-income Canadians find adequate and affordable housing no matter where they live in the country. To that end, in 1985 we entered into negotiations and an agreement called the Regina Accord, with all of the provinces of Canada including Quebec, which developed a formula for the distribution of federal social housing funds.
Under that formula, which Quebec signed and agreed to, Quebec's share of federal housing funds was set at

Government Orders
24.75 per cent of all of the units available. In fact, in the years between 1986 and 1989, Quebec received more than that share which it had agreed to in the formula and in fact, received 25.4 per cent of all of the units available.
In 1987, the provinces started to object to the formula. We tried to develop a new formula which all would agree to. We did agree to the fact that no matter where people lived in this country, they should all have access to assisted housing and, in effect, we agreed to national standards for housing across this country.
Unfortunately, there was no final agreement on all of the terms of the new formula. In 1990 I decided as a temporary measure only, without agreement of all parties, that we would put into effect the new formula. Under that new formula, we would respect the fundamental principles of needs and access for all Canadians, national standards.
Under that Quebec received in 1990, actually a larger share than it had before. Quebec now receives 25.65 per cent of all national housing units. In fact, that amounts to an increase in funding for Quebec for federal social housing dollars. In 1989, Quebec received some 18.31 per cent of the allocation, but in 1990 it received 5 per cent more, some 23.20 per cent, whereas Ontario which had received some 41 per cent of all of the federal social housing dollars in 1989, went down to some 35 per cent of social housing dollars in 1990.

I am the national minister of housing. As such, I have special responsibilities. Canada is a rich and civilized country. We must guarantee the quality of life of all our fellow citizens. We must ensure that their basic needs are met. As you know, food and housing are basic needs. I am firmly committed to helping the poor. I cannot let the administrative or political priorities of the various levels of government divert me from this responsibility and from the principle of equality which should motivate the actions of a national government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to resume the debate begun earlier.
I had started by making reference to the fact that what we are here to debate, of course, is the borrowing bill which is, in effect, an element of the budget though, in fact, it is something that exists under the Financial Administration Act.
Borrowing is about debt and it is about deficit. I hear all sorts of things said and played with about debt and deficit in this country. I think it is important to review the realities of the situation, to find out why it is necessary for the government to borrow money. A lot of people operate on the principle that the best way to run your affairs, whether they be government affairs or personal affairs, is to pay your bills as you go along. I am sure that is what most people want to do and that is certainly what any responsible government wants to do.
On the other hand, that is not what has been going on in Canada for the last decade or so. Consequently we are faced today with a staggering national debt, a debt that unfortunately is the legacy of our forebears. We are fortunate, however, in that for the past six and a half years, the country has benefited from a Minister of Finance who has made as his number one principle, his cardinal principle, fiscal responsibility and the coming to grips with the massive deficit he inherited.
When this government came into office in 1984, the annual deficit of this country had risen to $38 billion. That is a staggering amount of money. What is even more shocking, when one reflects on that, is that this deficit was not just interest payments, that in fact it included an $11 billion deficit in program spending. The government of the day was spending $11 billion more
March 5, 1991

than it was taking in in revenues. On top of that, this government and this Minister of Finance inherited $27 billion in interest charges every year.
My hon. friends opposite like to say: "Look at the way the national debt has grown under this government and under this minister." But it is a lot easier to say: "Get rid of the national deficit" than it is to do it. My hon. friends opposite are forever imploring this government to spend more. Every time there is a cost-cutting measure, we hear anguish and howling from the other side: "Why don't you spend more here?" We heard it in this debate during the course of today's session. On the other hand, any time the government takes a revenue-increasing measure-which of course is a lovely way of increasing the taxation load of Canadians, which is, in my opinion, too great-they say: "No, you cannot raise taxes either." So, you cannot raise taxes to deal with the deficit and you cannot reduce expenditures to deal with the deficit.
Then what do my hon. friends opposite do then? They turn around and criticize the government because we have a big deficit and a big debt.
How do you achieve rationality out of that? It is very simple. Canadians recognized some years ago that the only way to have rationality was to get a government that had a sense of fiscal responsibility, that had a recognition of the fact that you have to pay your bills in this world, and that recognized that ultimately down the road there is no such thing as a free lunch, that ultimately somebody is going to pay. And that is the government we have in power today.
When my hon. friends opposite suggest that we should not cut expenditures here or we should not raise taxes there, they never come up with a solution to the problem. Goodness knows what the shape of the deficit and the national debt would be in this country if my hon. friends opposite had continued the spendthrift ways that existed in this country from 1974 to 1984, when the average growth in program spending by the Government of Canada of the day-a government, I might say, not of my political persuasion-was 13.8 per cent. Since this government has been in power, that rate has been

reduced to 3.6 per cent, a remarkable improvement, which is below the level of inflation.
I believe that is a correct statement. I would not want to mislead the House.
The bottom line is that we have experienced fiscal responsibility.
When people say "cut", what do they mean? I go around my constituency and my province and people are always saying: "The government has to cut more spending." My impression of what people usually mean when they say to cut spending is to cut the programs that they are not interested in. Or if they say that you have to raise taxes, what they really mean is: "Raise the taxes that other people pay; don't raise the ones that I pay."
Fiscal responsibility means cutting the cloth according to the pattern in order that you can pay your bills. And that has been the hallmark of Mr. Wilson's period as Minister of Finance. The country's finances are in sufficiently good shape that we stand here debating a borrowing bill giving the government authority to borrow $26.4 billion. As the minister said to me the other day: "How do you figure out what $26 billion is? I cannot relate to that." He said: "I found out that they built the dome in Toronto for $500 million; that is half a billion. So, what I think of is 53 domes."
I hope the day will come when we do not need 53 domes or the money to purchase them.
The bottom line, Mr. Speaker, is that the progress that this government is making is such that we see a commitment that by 1994-95 we will have no further need for new borrowing by the Government of Canada. And that will be a very happy day for all Canadians.
The borrowing authority is in fact part of the government's budgetary plans. Let's take a look at those plans and see how they are put in place in such a way as to deal with this debt problem that the country has. What we saw in the budget the other night-and I must say that I thought it was an excellent budget brought forward by the Minister of Finance-is a budget that presents a clear plan for recovery and economic growth and renewal in this country. It will ultimately lead to lower interest rates which is going to be a benefit to all Canadians, I believe. It establishes clear and attainable inflation

Government Orders
targets and sets a clear path to a balanced budget, something we have not seen for many, many years in this country.
I want to say a word about interest rates. We used to hear members opposite, during the course of the last year, say: "ah, the government should arbitrarily lower interest rates". Well, you know, that was a politically popular thing to do. The government said: "Hey, if we just do that we get ourselves in a situation where we will simply fuel inflation, and that is not going to be for the benefit of Canadians". Inflation, in the final analysis, is the killer. We need investment in this country. Investment is attracted by people who have confidence in the economy.
The keys to the recovery and economic growth and development and fiscally responsible approach that this government is taking are several. First and foremost is control of government expenditures. This government has done this, as I said before, by getting a handle on those expenditures.
I mentioned that when Mr. Wilson became finance minister we had an $11 billion operating deficit in this country. That has been turned around to the point where it is now a $12.5 billion operating surplus. The reason in 1994-95 we are not going to need new government borrowing authority is because by then that operating surplus will be up to $22 billion. So we are making remarkable progress.
Now expenditure control may be responsible, but it is not always easy and it is not always popular. In the budget this year we have a freeze on program spending and a 3 per cent growth permissible thereafter in government spending. That is tough because we all know that costs are rising, so that if you are going to pull 3 per cent out it means you have got to find it from things that are there and that hurts.
I heard one of the hon. members opposite earlier today saying: "oh, it is terrible that we have had reductions here and reductions there". The fact of the matter is, given the interest rates from last year, in order to control inflation which is something clearly we are successfully doing, we had higher interest rates than we would have liked and the result was, of course, an increase in the interest pressure on the government debt charges. That meant that we would have had a deficit of $35 billion this year. Instead, through the restraint
program, we have brought that down to $30.5 billion and the finances of the country are in much better shape.
I think it is important symbolically as well as substantively that the government is not leading by saying this is what you should do, but leading by example. We are obviously not going to save a great deal of money in terms of the deficit by freezing cabinet ministers' salaries or by capping members, of Parliament salaries, but it sends the message that we, too, are prepared to share the burden. Similarly, with respect to the Public Service.
Now we have heard a tremendous amount of anguish expressed by leaders of the public service unions about the proposal in the budget that there be no increase in the budgetary allotment for salaries in the public service. That the government is not prepared to enter into a contractual arrangement in excess of 3 per cent and that if we go to the 3 per cent that is going to mean a comparable reduction in employees in order to make up the difference.
Well that is not a very happy circumstance, but the fact of the matter is that the government cannot preach to private industry, it cannot preach to the provinces unless it is prepared to set the example itself.
I heard a member opposite the other day lamenting the fact that salaries in the Public Service were barely an average of $30,000 a year. Well I would like to say that there are an awful lot of fish plant workers in the South Shore constituency, there are an awful lot of Christmas tree harvesters in the South Shore constituency who would be more than pleased to try to get along on $30,000 a year. So I think things sometimes have to be put into perspective.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are telling me that my time is almost up and I am barely getting warmed up, but I do want to mention one thing before I conclude and that is with respect to the subject of grants and contributions where there is to be a $75 million reduction in expenditures.
I think non-governmental organizations play an important role in Canada. I am not always convinced that we have to give out, as government, all the grants that we do, but I think there are certain principles that should be followed in determining where these cuts should be made. First of all, it is fashionable to say cut core funding and just fund projects. Well, having been president of a national NGO for three years I can tell you that if they will not provide you with core funding then you spend all
March 5, 1991

your time trying to stay alive and cannot get on with the work you are put there to do.
Secondly, we have to look at which NGOs have the potential to fund-raise. Some do, some do not. That is a principle we should look at.
Finally we should look at the federal mandate and policy objectives and make sure we support objectives which Canadians feel to be desirable.
Mr. Speaker, I see you are giving me the sign so I guess I must adjourn. If I may just mention in closing that it is extremely important that this bill pass expeditiously because borrowing authority extends to March 31 from last year's bill. If we do not get a new borrowing authority bill we are then faced with short-term financing which will cost the taxpayers of Canada a lot of money that we need not spend. Therefore, I commend the bill to all members and urge their support of it.

This government is already deeply enough in debt on borrowed time. If this government wanted to serve the people of this country, what it would do is resign right now.
I listened to the Prime Minister deliver his constitutional talk to the Empire and Canadian Clubs in Toronto and I listened to his vision for dealing with the question of Canadian unity, of its future Constitution, and his solution to the problems that are plaguing the country and causing such great concern to Canadians. I want to read a portion of this speech because I think it is important for Canadians to understand what he is up to, what he has been up to, and what he will be up to.
He set out I think seven characteristics that would govern constitutional change in this country. He said that the first benchmark of that future reconstitution of this nation would be to build the kind of prosperous Canada that his government has been in the process of building.
Let us understand specifically what that means because I think it is going to frighten Canadians when they understand what he considers to be fundamental to any constitutional change. That is that those gains that have been achieved by the free trade agreement, privatization and fiscal changes such as the goods and services tax are

the first prerequisite in this man's vision of the future of Canada.
Evidently, he is completely immune to the fact that what he has already been engaged in, in terms of that economic policy, lies at the very basis of the constitutional crisis in this country, because every Canadian has the presumption that he has been involved in the destruction of this nation. That is why we have a constitutional crisis.
Let us look at the record of this economic policy. First of all, that economic policy has been marked with a closer identification with American values. This is in some respects exemplified in the free trade agreement, the specific intent of which is to bring a greater degree of harmonization between our two nations. It really is a reflection of the Prime Minister's personal identification with a philosophy that is exclusively market-driven. It is a point of view that leads Canada to be the lap-dog of American foreign policy, as well as its economic mimic.
Someone said that when the Prime Minister went to New York when he was first elected Prime Minister of this country he came, he saw, he concurred.
An important part of this Americanization of Canada, the hurtful part of this Americanization of Canada, has been the attack on those institutions and programs which to the Canadian mind has kept this country together with a sense of community. It is a nation that extends across the vast geographic area, that consists of any number of different populations requiring certain kinds of institutions to keep them together such as the CBC, VIA Rail, the post office. All of these things have been under attack.
Social programs have been under attack. Medicare is under attack. Even in Quebec, even among those who are not sure of the future relationship that Quebec should have with Canada, the attack on medicare has been regarded, even there, as an attack on the Confederation of Canada.
Then we have the strange approach to economic growth, which in fact is completely contradictory to everything that they have said about improving Canada's competitiveness in the world.

After all, the deficit reflects the ability of the country to produce wealth and therefore to what degree taxes are collected and in what amounts. It reflects the payments that have to be made to those who are not working. It is clear that the deficit is not just a fiscal measure. It must reflect economic measures as well, but this government has failed to choose those appropriate measures that will address the economy and, over the long run, address the deficit.
The budget, with its attack and preoccupation with the deficit, is a reflection of a mentality: the bookkeeper's mentality, the economists mentality, the bottom line mentality. If I wanted to compare what the Minister of Finance has done, I think what I would want to cite is the example of the automobile industry 10 years ago, in which accountants like the finance minister and others on that side were so preoccupied with the bottom line and circumstances when they could get away with it that they started getting rid of their engineers, their scientists, their designers, their creative people. Yes, they are still getting a profit, but across the Pacific Ocean the designers, the engineers and the scientists-the people who do creative work, not the accountants-were producing cars that created a field of competition that required change. They had to look at the roles of creativity, of innovation, of knowledge, and of technology in the automobile industry.
We can extend that analogy to this nation. This has become a bottom-line nation in a world of knowledge, technology, creativity and ability to produce value added combined to produce wealth. This country is falling increasingly far behind and has been doing so ever since this government came into office. The strange and bizarre thing is that the Prime Minister seemed to recognize back in 1983 the necessity of doing something about Canada's utter failure in the areas of research, development, technology and innovation.
This budget continues the tack that has not only failed to meet the measure of improvement, but the Prime Minister's promise has still further eroded our ability as a nation to create the kind of value-added economy we are going to need to have to compete.
What are the dimensions of this? Specifically, we must have increased investment in research and development. We must have more scientists, more engineers and a more highly-trained work force. We must have, therefore, improvements and not a deterioration in post-secondary education. We must have improvements and not a deterioration of the levels of training, and we must make investments in infrastructure.
Yes, what has happened? It goes on. If we look at research and development, for example, the National Research Council will get an increase of roughly 3 per cent. It is kind of difficult to calculate with any precision, but roughly 3 per cent. In fact, before the budget was released the National Research Council received a message from the finance minister that it could be assured of an increase in funding of $50 million over the next five years.
This is the same NRC that this government cut back in 1985-86. This is the same NRC that has had its scientific complement cut over the last year by about 100. This is the same NRC that submitted a proposed five-year plan last spring in which it asked for $125 million over five years for IRAP alone, that is the Industrial Research Assistance Program. Let us look at the comparison: $50 million over five years of which the 3 per cent increase received in the budget is applied. For the entire NRC, as compared to $125 million asked for over five years for IRAP, the most successful job producing program the government finances anywhere at $15,000 a job.
Yet, the government did not see fit to take money for its advertising of the GST and all those other wasteful expenditures and put it where the proper priorities would have had it.

The National Advisory Board for Science and Technology and the House committee on industry, science and technology, on which you might realize, Mr. Speaker, there are a couple of government members, agreed that the funding for the granting councils which support basic research in universities should be doubled over a three-year period. It is important to have up-to-date equipment both for competitiveness and forefront research and for training graduate students. Finally, with respect to infrastructure, we find that this government has failed utterly to recognize the importance in our municipalities, our provinces and our

regions of infrastructure for the success of future economic development in this country.
Robert Reich has described two kinds of approaches to an economy. You can have a vicious cycle that is based on the premise that you can achieve economic development by offering a good business environment. That is kind of familiar, meaning low wages, few regulations and low taxes especially for the rich. You can have a virtuous cycle, he says, of economic development if you adopt the premise that you are going to educate your workers and you are going to encourage creativity. Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to make a few comments in respect of Bill C-97, the borrowing bill, which obviously relates directly to the budget recently brought down by the Minister of Finance.
Also, it relates directly to my own responsibilities, my own portfolio, and the impact that this bill and the budget has on housing, on our national housing programs and on the federal housing agency, Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
You and I well know, Mr. Speaker, the difficult problem that faced the Minister of Finance in trying to address the economic situation in a budget this year. On the one hand, there was an enormous deficit situation, a situation which had grown more severe in this past year, on top of a very substantial national debt.
Balancing that situation were economic difficulties in the country which have to be addressed as well. Somehow or other, the Minister of Finance had to meet the debt problem and, at the same time, meet the economic difficulties we have in the country.
I believe that he has managed to do that in a way that has not hurt or damaged those who are the poor and the disadvantaged people in this country, particularly as that applies to housing. It was not an easy task. I have to congratulate him for the job he did with respect to dealing with the housing budget and with people who need help in housing.
In fact, the bottom line of the budget is that in spite of a continuing 15 per cent reduction in ongoing increases in social housing spending-a reduction that was put into place in last year's budget, through this year and on for the fiscal framework of the next five years-this year the actual amount of money the federal government will be spending on social housing is going up by $116 million.

March 5, 1991
Government Orders
That is added to the amounts that were spent last year and in previous years. This extra amount includes an inflationary increase which will go into effect and will allow us to continue to maintain the existing assisted housing program across our country. That inflationary increase to help existing housing programs amounts to some $30 million of additional money.
Added to that is an additional $86 million which will allow the federal government, through the federal housing agency, CMEIC, to help to assist even more people who need housing and help with housing in this country in the coming year.
I trust that all members of the House are aware that currently across the country the federal government is assisting almost 650,000 needy households. These are people who fall into the categories of senior citizens and single parent families, the majority of whom are women-led single parent families. They fall into the categories of disabled people, low income single women, families with low incomes, single people with low incomes, disabled people with low incomes and natives with low incomes.
It is interesting to note that this help is directed towards Canadians who this year will have an average annual income of around $11,000 a year only. Therefore, this sum is being spent to assist people like that. It is certainly very needed and certainly very helpful.
Again, I think the Minister of Finance is to be congratulated for making sure that this budget does not impact on those people any more severely than it has in the past, and in fact will be helping over 40,000 more needy households this year than were helped last year.
It is important to recognize as well that the budget is going to allow for the continuation of all of our national housing programs, and, in particular, will allow for the continuation of some housing programs which we hope to improve this year.
One of those is what is known as our RRAP program, our Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program. It helps natives living on reserves, it helps low-income homeowners and it helps people with disabilities who are homeowners as well.
In 1990, the federal government was able to assist some 25,000 households under this program. This was done through a forgivable loan program which involved some $105 million and which allowed people whose housing had fallen below standard to upgrade their homes and to continue to live in those homes. This program helps very dramatically, very inexpensively and cost effectively Canadians who own homes but who need help to maintain them. If they do not get that help, they are going to have to move into other assisted housing that some government would have to build from scratch.
This is a very cost-effective program. It is one we have been reviewing over the last few years and I expect we will be coming forward with some new suggestions in the coming year. Perhaps there will be a suggestion that I know my colleagues in the House from the province of Quebec are most interested in and that is helping low-income people who rent. Our past program, which was discontinued two years ago, the rental RAP program, is being looked at to see if there is some way that we could provide some help in this area. That help will go to needy people and not to investors or people who can afford to make these repairs on their own.
Another program we hope we will be making some additions to this year is our rural and native housing program. This program has been targeted to natives living off reserve and to people in remote and rural areas of the country. Some 50 per cent of all of the funds under that program have been targeted over the last few years to natives. We again expect that in the coming year, after completing a consultation process and an evaluation process of those programs that we will be coming forward with some new suggestions as to how we can improve that program as well.
One of the programs we have already improved is one that I announced a week ago yesterday, and that was a new and augmented initiative in the area of housing for the victims of family violence. This, of course, includes the women and the children who are victims of family violence. It also includes senior citizens. It also includes disabled people who, as you know, are these days the subject of family violence, something which all of us feel very deeply is completely and totally unacceptable in our society. As a result, not only must we try to prevent family violence from occurring, we must deal with the effects, the impact of family violence. We have to

provide some housing, whether it is emergency shelters for the victims of family violence or whether it is longer term housing after they have had a short stay in an emergency shelter.
The government already has in place a program called Project Haven, which started in 1988 and should conclude in 1992. Over that time we should be able to put in place another 450 emergency shelter units to help the victims of family violence.
A week ago yesterday I announced in Edmonton an augmentation of that program whereby we would provide a further $4 million for shelters and a further $16 million for second-stage housing for the victims of family violence. I do not think I have to say that housing is one of the very basic concerns Canadians have. It is what I refer to as one of the fundamentals, one of the cornerstones of Canadian society. As such, I believe very deeply that it is necessary for us to maintain into the future, as we now have, national standards in housing. We have to make sure that we allow people to become homeowners, because that is one of the deep-felt yearnings that binds us together as Canadians, that feeling that we want to be able to own our own home. Many people came to this country because they wanted to be homeowners.
In addition, we have to make sure that those who cannot afford to be homeowners, those who cannot afford to look after all of their housing needs, have decent and affordable housing wherever they live in this country, whether it is in urban areas, whether it is in rural areas, or in the remote north. Every needy Canadian who just cannot afford to provide decent, affordable housing for themselves has that opportunity. That is why we need to have national standards in housing.
Government Orders
In the debate on national unity which is under way right now and as we examine the question of the division of powers between the federal Parliament and provincial legislatures, one of the things we must bear in mind in this debate is the need for national standards in housing that apply right across this country.
One of the important aspects of the budget which ties in with the bill we are debating this evening, is the fact that all of the items in the budget are aimed at trying to bring down interest rates. It is obviously a very essential part of helping housing in this country.
It is interesting to note that a drop of 1 per cent in interest rates allows approximately 100,000 more Canadians to become homeowners. It makes housing affordable for 100,000 more Canadians with the drop of 1 percentage point in interest rates. In fact, over the last few months, I think it was about June or July of this year, you will have noted that mortgage interest rates had reached some 14.25 per cent. Now that is still far below the 22 per cent to 23 per cent that mortgage interest rates reached in the early 1980s, but at the same time, there has been a drop since June and July from a 14.25 per cent mortgage interest rate to an 11 per cent mortgage interest rate today. That has meant a veiy substantial difference in the affordability of housing. In fact, it means that the average person buying a house and paying mortgage payments on a $100,000 mortgage is in fact paying about $250 a month less than they were paying a few short months ago.
All of this is extremely important in encouraging housing and, of course, the building of housing and the improvement of the real estate market. All of that, of course, is what the budget is aimed at and, I think, aimed at quite successfully.
We are going to be doing some other things in this coming year as well and I would just like to comment on two of those very briefly. One of them is that I hope to be bringing forward some amendments to the National Housing Act which will allow the mortgage insurance fund of CMHC to ensure shared-equity home purchases. I expect, and very shortly will be announcing, the creation of a Canadian housing partnership centre which will take the initiative and act as a catalyst in developing public-private housing partnerships so that we can do more with the funds that we have available in providing badly needed assisted housing for Canadians.
At the same time, in this coming year we are going to be putting into effect some cost efficiencies and cost reductions which will allow us to continue to do and to help another 40,000 more Canadians next year much more than we are helping at the present time.
In conclusion, I just want to say that I believe that the budget that has been brought down by the Minister of Finance has created a delicate balance here, and, quite successfully, one which is going to lower interest rates, lower inflation, lower the deficit, increase economic confidence and, in doing so, it is going to give a boost to housing.
As you know, housing means strong families, strong communities, a strong economy and a strong nation.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak about this bill, with particular reference to the budget's affect on my riding of Kent, and southern Ontario as a whole.

Government Orders
Southern Ontario is the economic engine of Canada; in fact, southwestern Ontario alone is responsible for 60 per cent of the province's gross domestic product.
This is no ordinary recession. The government's economic policies are hitting southern Ontario hard. Plants are closing down and jobs are lost forever. It is a far ciy from the temporary examples of the last recession of 1981 and 1982.
We know that an economy, like an engine, cannot keep revving at high RPMs forever. You cannot sustain a hundred miles an hour. But with proper upkeep and good maintenance the engine will be ready to fire again. But this government is a group of very poor mechanics. Its policies are putting up roadblocks and southern Ontario is seizing up with the twin-engine killers of high interest rates and a high dollar.
For those who say that this recession may be bad but it definitely is better than the last one, they are dead wrong. The welfare rates in Kent County are up 400 per cent from 1981 levels. The city of Chatham has a 30 per cent unemployment rate in the automotive sector. Companies such as Motor Wheel Corporation are closing their doors. That plant has been in Chatham ever since I was a young child, and we have been through tough times before. The Hunt-Wesson tomato canning plant in Tilbury closed down last year after being in operation for over 25 years. That plant and its workers made it through the last recession but not this one.
The blame lies in the high interest, high dollar, and free trade policy of this government.
I point out, Mr. Speaker, that it is not me who says that. It is not the unions who say that. It was Hunt-Wesson's president who said that. Those jobs are going to California and to Ohio, with tomato farmers in my riding left holding their baskets.
Before, Canada was armed for the wars of recession, but with free trade our guns are checked at the border and we now have no protection from the gunslingers of big corporate America.
A fact that should not be overlooked as well is that in the 1982 recession only 24 per cent of the layoffs involved total or partial plant closings. But in 1990 these accounted for 64 per cent of the job cuts.
This is not the same as 1981-1982. The impact of the recession is hitting everywhere.
In Dresden, population 2,500, two of its most major employers are closing their doors, over 100 jobs eliminated. Think of the ripple effect on the local economy.
In Chatham, at truck builder Navistar nearly one-quarter of its 800 strong workforce is laid off. Seimens, a world-class company with more than 1,000 employees now has nearly a third on lay-off.
But the biggest blow is the impending closure of Motor Wheel where only 250 remain of a workforce that once totalled over 600. The plant is shutting its doors in May.
About a third of Chatham's workforce is in the auto parts industry so it would follow that the city would suffer similar setbacks as other auto towns such as Windsor and Oshawa. But Chatham is smaller with a population of only 42,000 and when a plant lays off the result devastates and disrupts the entire local economy.
The lay-offs have had a dramatic effect on the city. Real estate sales are down 50 per cent. Bankruptcies handled by just one office of Peat Marwick Thome in Chatham are up 50 per cent from last year.
Kent County is home of the Ontario tax revolt and it can only balloon after this budget. To compensate for the loss of federal transfer support the provinces and municipalities are either going to increase taxes or cut services.
Federal inaction could result in more bed closings at hospitals, even longer waiting lists for surgery, a poorer education system, and less money for roads and infrastructure.
The finance minister has actually suggested that provincial road budgets should be reduced. He must not do much driving on the 401 highway.
Modem highways and transportation routes are absolutely crucial to southern Ontario with their "just in time" industries. Improved routes to help our industries should be a priority not an afterthought.
This is no ordinary recession. The town of Dresden, ever since I can remember, always had about four or five farm implement dealers. Those small businessmen made it through 1981-1982, but not this time. Now there are none left-zero.
March 5, 1991

The working people see federal tax revenues up 70 per cent since 1984.
This is the stuff of which tax revolts are made. Canadian households will pay a total of $11.1 billion more in federal taxes, net of transfers, than they would if the 1984 tax system were still in place. An average Canadian family is paying about $1,000 more through this government's policies.
This is a government that promised in its first budget an $18 billion deficit this year. After six years of tax increases, program cutbacks and global economic growth, the government is having great difficulty explaining why the deficit is still increasing and the public debt is out of control.
In 1981 Canada followed the rest of the world into recession. This time we plunged into recession fully eight months before the U.S., creating the first "made in Canada" recession. The recession is cutting deeper into the economic foundation of southwestern Ontario.
The finance minister calls his budget a prosperity challenge. For most Canadians it is going to be a survival challenge. The years ahead will see the fiercest competition the world has ever known but we need the tools to do it. The government's actions are taking us in the other direction. We are witnessing the terrible deindustrialization of Canada. We have lost 229,000 jobs or 11 per cent of all manufacturing jobs since free trade.
The Canadian Manufacturers' Association has shown that the ability of Canada to compete with its major trading partners is only 85 per cent of what it was in 1980. We have lost 20 per cent of our share of the world markets during the last five years.
The trade balance with our major trading partner, the U.S., has dropped $6 billion since 1984. Further, our current account balance with our neighbours to the south has been ripped from a positive balance of $6.7 billion in 1984 to a $2.7 billion deficit in 1989.
These are certainly not the results that government is looking for, after saying we should be competitive.
As our industrial sectors are being sacked and pillaged through free trade and a sad economy, the Tory government has offered no adjustment programs to deal with the restructuring.
Government Orders
Canada is facing a serious long-term competitive crisis, and it is no more apparent than in southwestern Ontario. Southern Ontario, Canada's manufacturing heartland, is suffering from hardening of the arteries. As the winds of change blow away our economic structures and erode southern Ontario's foundation, the government is standing back and watching. Any good farmer knows that you do not just stand back and watch your soil erode and blow away. You set up windbreaks.
Our manufacturing sector is the soil by which Canada's economy grows and prospers. The Tory government is letting it erode.
Recession is not just a word in the dictionary. If affects your neighbour across the backyard fence, the farmer down the road, and the local coffee shop where everyone gathers at six in the morning. It affects your kid's hockey and baseball coach. Recession hits families.
To conclude, this is no ordinary recession. There is a tax revolt in Kent County as the Conservatives, through this budget, place more of the burden on the provinces and municipalities. Welfare rates in Kent Country are zooming, burdened by the weight of the recession.
No, this is no ordinary recession. The economic engine of southwestern Ontario is seizing up. The budget presented last week offers no tune-up, no answers, just more of the same. Our economic foundation is being wrenched away. Plants are closing down. Jobs are lost forever.
We need a government that is sensitive to the changes going on around us, one that will stick up for the little guy and will lend a helping hand to workers and their families.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak on the government's borrowing bill and to raise certain economic issues of concern to northern Canada.
With this bill, Parliament is being asked to spend and to approve the government's spending plan. Parliament is being asked to approve an awful lot of money with this bill but very little of the government's proposed expenditures, as we learn in this budget, will address the most pressing social and economic needs of the aboriginal and northern people.
When the Minister of Finance tabled his budget a week ago, he announced that Inuit and Indian programs would be exempt from the extension of the government's expenditure control plan, which sounds very good on the surface, but we still do not know the extent of that exemption. The Minister of Finance neglected to tell this House and the people of Canada that the Indian and Inuit programs were capped for two years in last year's budget. There were some exemptions for health, education, social assistance and claims, but these programs were not exempted out of the goodness of the federal government's heart.
The federal government has a legal obligation to provide health, education, social assistance, and claims funding to aboriginal people. The question we have is: Does the extension of the exemption apply only to these programs which the federal government is legally obliged to provide? The answer is not clear. Even the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development was not sure last week.
As I said earlier, last year's budget cap on Indian and Inuit programs was for two years. The cap on Indian and Inuit programs is in effect this year as it was last year.
Government Orders
This fact, the Minister of Finance neglected to mention in his speech.
I will remind the house that this cap on Indian and Inuit programs means the loss of $100 million to Indian and Inuit programs. The minister's own budget documents from last year display these figures in black and white. Last year $50 million was lost, and this year another $50 million is being cut.
The government is not restoring this lost $100 million. As I said earlier, we do not yet know how much the recently announced exemption covers.
Last year's budget strangled aboriginal organizations and aboriginal communications. The pattern continues this year.
Last year the core operating funding for the aboriginal organizations in this country was cut severely. This year it has been cut again.
The government's borrowing bill does not restore any funding to aboriginal organizations or aboriginal communications. Government's borrowing bill does not provide any additional funding to Canada Post for the food mail program.
Since the fall we have been waiting for a report from the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development on this issue, and we have yet to see it. When are we going to see this report?
The territorial government has had its transfer payments cut back by this government. The Yukon government will receive about $80 million less over a five-year period than it would otherwise have received from the federal government. The Northwest Territories will receive about $100 million less over the same time period. In 1991-1992, there is a loss of about $30 million in federal transfer payments to the Government of the Northwest Territories.
It has become abundantly clear that this federal government does not have an economic plan for the north. The government does not recognize the unique social and economic development needs of the north. Investing in the north is not a priority of this government.
The government produced a document in 1988 called A Northern Political and Economic Framework, but nothing is happening under this framework that is improving the daily lives of people in the north. Instead, the north

Government Orders
has seen only cutbacks and federal policies which discriminate against the north.
For example, we have seen in the past few years cutbacks in the funding formula for transfers to the territories, a tightening in the unemployment insurance program, a substantial weakening of the tax benefits provided to mining by the elimination of flow-through shares, previous increases in the sales tax burden on air transportation and telecommunication services, the imposition of the GST and others.
The 1991 federal budget is just the latest example of this federal government's anti-northern bias. The budget makes cuts to the environment, to the Canadian Jobs Strategy; to housing and to aboriginal organizations. It provides no help, no hope and no relief.
Instead, northerners are being told that they will have to continue to suffer. We have serious housing problems in the Northwest Territories. We have homelessness. We have overcrowding. We have social problems and health problems as a result, but the budget does nothing to alleviate these problems. Instead, it cuts back on the spending for social housing.
We have serious unemployment problems in the north, especially among our youth. This budget does nothing to help the unemployed. Instead, it cuts back on job training funds.
The north desperately needs regionally appropriate and culturally appropriate education and training programs. Forty per cent of the population of the Northwest Territories is under the age of 19. Where is the help for these young people? There are no jobs. Where is the forward thinking that would see our youth as our future? Why has this federal government not invested in our youth?
Last April, this House unanimously approved to support my private member's motion on aboriginal youth. The government has not acted on my motion even though, as I said, it was unanimously approved.
Our aboriginal youth have the highest suicide rate in this country. There are serious social problems, but there is little or no help from the federal government. The government has no vision for the north. It does not listen to the people of the north.
When this government makes economic policy, northern Canada and northern Canadians are left out. Our geography places us far away from the centre of Canada. Our population is small compared to southern Canada, but our geography and population are not reason to leave us on the fringe of federal, political, and economic decision-making. Not only are we on the fringe of this government's decision-making; we do not even get the fringe benefits that normally flow from being a Canadian.
There is a significant gap in the levels of services in the north compared to the rest of Canada. The borrowing bill and the budget will not reduce these gaps, and these gaps will likely increase.
Infrastructural needs in the north have barely been addressed. Yet, basic infrastructure is a necessary precondition to the development of a self-sustaining northern economy. We lack transportation infrastructures. There are no roads linking communities in my constituency. We cannot reduce our high cost of living and our business operating costs without basic infrastructure. Our community infrastructure needs expansion and upgrading.
Substantial catch-up funding is also required to bring standards of some educational and health facilities in line with those of the average Canadian. There are seven communities in the Keewatin region and no hospitals. There are nine communities in the Kitikmeot region and no hospital. There are 14 communities in the Baffin region and one hospital.
Our unemployment rates are staggering. The Government of the Northwest Territories is projecting an over-all unemployment rate of 24 per cent and a native unemployment rate of 40 per cent by the year 2000. Yet, there are only two Canada employment and immigration offices in a constituency serving 36 communities. The Keewatin region has one, the Baffin region has one. The Kitikmeot region has none. I want to use this opportunity, on behalf of the residents of the Kitikmeot region, to urge the federal government to establish a Canada employment office there.
Where is the Arctic environmental strategy? In December, when the government tabled its green plan, the Arctic environmental strategy was missing. Last week, the Minister of Finance cut $125 million from the green plan by stretching its planned spending from five to six years. Major elements of the Arctic environmental

strategy are supposed to deal with Arctic contaminants and waste clean-up. The green plan itself recognized that it was most urgent to protect the Arctic ecosystem.
In conclusion, we need action now. The federal government must make a commitment to the sustainable development of northern Canada.
A few weeks ago, several of my colleagues in the Official Opposition spent some time in the north with me listening to northerners about the economic situation. The government's policies and its latest budget are contributing to the creation of an Arctic ghetto.
I urge this government to reverse this course before it is too late.
