Mr. Speaker, before getting into the main thrust of my remarks tonight, I would like to respond to a number of comments made by the hon. member for Nunatsiaq when he painted a rather bleak picture of life in his region, in the North.
I would like to point out to the hon. member that in my riding there are native communities all along the north shore of the Saint-Lawrence. These communities, Mr. Speaker, achieved a lot in the past few years. They got involved in their economic development, their housing development, as well as their development in the fields of health and education. They created organizations to
achieve the objectives they have set and to improve substantially their living conditions.
I also had the privilege of visiting a few northern localities of my riding, along the Bay of Ungava. There too, Mr. Speaker, great strides were made. Since 1984, this government pumped considerable amounts into the development of the communities and institutions of the northerners.
That being said, Mr. Speaker, I would like to revert to the main thrust of my speech and tell you that this opportunity to speak on Bill C-97 will allow me to reflect tonight on certain very important aspects of the budget presented by the Minister of Finance. The borrowing authority requested is anticipating on the financial needs of the govemement, needs that in turn depend in part on the efficiency of the measures which the government is going to take to control expenditures.
Since it came to power in 1984, this government has recognized that its first financial responsibilities lay with its own operations. Its operating expenditures have been severely restricted and even reduced in real terms.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians expect that the government and its civil servants also be subjected to restrictions in hard times. But most important, federal politicians and civil servants are requested to accept wage restraints in order to set an example during these difficult times. Wage settlements in the public sector should not increase inflationary pressures upon the economy. That is why the government shows moderation in its wage settlements while maintaining the principles of collective bargaining.
In fact, since 1987, wage settlements within the federal administration have been lower than those of the provincial, municipal, or private sectors, Mr. Speaker. In this period of recession, other restraints are necessary. The 1991 budget announced new spending cuts and measures to improve efficiency. The Prime Minister's remuneration as well as his cabinet members' salaries have been frozen for a year while the hon. members' wages are subjected to stringent limitations. The wage budgets of departments will not be adjusted for any increases in costs arising out of new collective agreements.
The government is not prepared either, Mr. Speaker, over the next three years, to consider wage increases beyond 3 per cent at an annual rate. Rates of salary increase for senior civil servants, deputy ministers, and

Crown corporation managers will be limited to a level not exceeding the average of negotiated settlements in the federal public service.
We will eliminate layers of management and reduce by 10 per cent the number of senior managers in the public service. Finally, next year capital spending and new-wage operating budgets will be frozen at their 1990-91 levels and subsequently we will strictly control their growth. This reduction program will allow savings of $3.6 billion over the next five years.
Mr. Speaker, all government levels must assume their responsibilities in that area, because we are all serving the same taxpayer. Moreover, we will all benefit from the alleviation of inflationary pressures under the form of lower interest rates, more vigorous growth, and greater job creation. Wage restrictions are particularly important at the provincial and municipal levels, more so in education and health care because the wage settlements increased at a faster rate than inflation in those sectors.
Wage settlements concluded in the private sector have also contributed to inflationary tensions. The reduction of those tensions will help in lowering interest rates, down, reducing costs, and improving competitiveness. There will follow a more rapid growth, new jobs and higher revenue.
Mr. Speaker, we must remember that the more dynamic economy that is the goal of those measures will allow the government to move faster towards deficit reduction and debt control. The spontaneous reaction to the request of $26 billion that is made in Bill C-97 is one of consternation, but the legislation only reflects the reality of government finances at this time. I prefer to take a positive approach to the issue, remembering that without the budget, a much greater amount would have been required.
Mr. Speaker, we should also remember that the last budget contained legislative measures that restricted government expenditures. This is the first time for a government to introduce such measures in a budget. It is an extremely important measure which will force all governments, present and future, to limit by an act of law the growth of expenditures.

Certain members also said, Mr. Speaker, these last few days, that transfer payments to provinces will not increase. This is not true, Mr. Speaker. Transfer payments will indeed increase, but at a slower rate than expected. Nevertheless, these increases represent 3.7 per cent or at last 3 per cent to 4 per cent of the amounts projected for the transfer payments to provinces.
These are measures which must be mentioned. These are positive aspects, and it is not right to say that this year's budget is completely negative for the economy. On the contrary, it is a budget designed to stimulate the economy. It is a budget which proposes spending cuts. It is a budget which is extremely selective in the additional charges it imposes on Canadian taxpayers. I believe it is a budget which will be approved by all Canadians and economic sectors, because it reflects accurately Canada's economic state.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that my colleagues approve this bill without delay. We must let the committee go to work right now and study the bill in order that it can be adopted as fast as possible. This is necessary to ensure the smooth operation of public finances and to keep control over the government's borrowing.

This is parallel to his famous line on the way to resolve the constitutional crisis: "When the car is in the ditch, you go back and forth and back and, eventually, you get it out". Except that some people manage to drive the car right off the road. It was probably something like the solution he had in mind during the Oka crisis when he suggested: "Let the Warriors go and arrest them later.
It was probably something like the solution he advocated to settle the Persian Gulf crisis not so long ago when he said: "Well, it is not all that bad, we ought to give Saddam Hussein a chance to save face.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the kind of contradictory statements we hear. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance have been quite clear about the extra revenue the GST will bring in as compared with the manufacturers' sales tax. When the current leader of the Liberal Party was representing my riding, that tax cost hundreds and hundreds of jobs because the industries in Shawini-gan and Grand'Mere were no longer competitive.
We did away with that tax, Mr. Speaker, and replaced it by a modem tax which is in force in socialist countries like Sweden and France. I was in Belgium recently and people there were telling me: "We cannot understand what is going on. I am strongly in favour of rebuilding our country, Canada, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, this is the finance minister's seventh budget and the first delivered during a recession, although looking at the minister's previous budgets it can be said that each one has contributed directly to the conditions under which we now find ourselves. The projections of the Minister of Finance and Treasury Board are completely out of whack with reality. The budget offers no solutions to Canada's poor, sick, unemployed, and homeless.

The good news, yes, there is even one bit of good news in this budget, is that it may be the Minister of Finance's last budget, and that is where it ends.
Some of the minister's promoters say that this budget is intended to be the cornerstone of his legacy as Minister of Finance, but, for the life of me, I cannot see why. This budget is only the latest in a litany of measures that have not worked, have been painful for Canadians and have resulted in Canadians losing their homes, their jobs, and their sense of national pride in terms of what Canada means to them in institutions, in symbols and in universality. Like all of his budgets, this one erodes that vision and that philosophy of Canada even more.
Among other things, this is a budget that continues the government's assault on health care and education in Canada. By freezing contributions to the provinces and capping other transfers, the government is altering the balance in this country which seeks to provide equality for the provinces and equality for Canadian citizens no matter where they live, no matter where they work, no matter what their income, and no matter what their status is in life.
Through all seven Conservative budgets, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance have attempted to show us that they are competent and that they care about the institutions of this country and are prepared to put a caring feeling into the fiscal policies. However, Canadians have realized that this budget is the same as all the others before. They can see that behind the rhetoric of the strong economic policies and the catch-all phrases like stability, a positive environment, and economic strength, there is nothing. These phrases are meant to convey an image which is false.
I like to refer to it as a hologram budget, an image of economic make-believe which Canadians can walk and see right through. In this light, I can agree with the minister's supporters that the budget is an icon for future Ministers of Finance to follow. It will be a legacy carved in stone, a testament to economic mismanagement that unfortunately is something his disciples here on the other side will have to wrestle with.
The Conservative government propped itself up on the belief that it could provide strong economic policies to ensure Canada's competitiveness the world over. It claimed that by getting government out of their lives, out of the lives of Canadians, in effect deregulating govern-

March 5, 1991
Government Orders
ment, it would save a pile of money and that Canadians would be better off, although it never said exactly how nor when this would happen.
In spite of these claims, as a former journalist, I can say that such claims must be weighed against the evidence in order to verify the truth. This deregulation is not the panacea it is hailed to be. The Conservative government thought that all it had to do was point to the United States in order to see the benefits of this practice. There, deregulation had another name; Reaganomics.
In his new book about the legacy of the Reagan years entitled Within Our Means-The Struggle for Economic Recovery After a Reckless Decade, Alfred Malabre concludes that: "Most of the problems that festered under Reagan grew worse from the pile-up of the debt to the deteriorization of health care and to the decay of the infrastructure. New problems arose".
Sound familiar, Mr. Speaker? Canada's national debt piled up to over $400 billion dollars, doubled since the Conservatives took office in 1984. The deteriorization of health care is also upon us, courtesy of the minister's latest budget, and the decay in our country's infrastructure can be seen in the gaping holes of Canada's social safety net.
Deregulation in Canada was taken by the Conservatives to mean that it was okay to deregulate the federal government, okay to deregulate our national institutions, okay to deregulate our social safety net, because that is exactly what the Conservative government has done over the last six and a half years of being here in office.
I asked the member for South Shore to give us an explanation, of which he could not, and I will say again that it is about time that this government took responsibility for its own economic and fiscal mismanagement, without excuses, for the national debt that has to have been allowed to double under this government. This government experienced over six years of the most prosperous years in Canada in recent times and it could not control the national debt nor the deficit.
The Minister of Finance predicted in his first budget of 1985 that by the fiscal year 1991-1992 the deficit would have been brought down to $18 billion. In the budget of 1991-1992 the minister instead predicted a deficit of $30.5 billion. Even in his latest attempt at diversion, the Minister of Finance says that things should not be as bad within the next few years because inflation will come down to 2 per cent.
What hat did the minister pull that figure out of? Even in the best of times-and I think the minister hopes things will get a little better-inflation just cannot get that low. The minister had predicted that the inflation rate would only rise slightly once the GST came into effect. But what happened? The inflation rate jumped to an incredible 6.8 per cent.
The minister had based the current budget projections over the next five years on the belief that inflation would go down to 2 per cent. All I can say is that he should bring in a new budget which reflects reality.
Suddenly the Minister of Finance announces in his budget that under the new legislation government departmental budgets will be spelled out in black ink, and that the GST revenues would be allocated solely to reducing the deficit. That is contrary to the minister's statement that the GST would be revenue neutral. Remember we all heard that. Of course that was misleading. After ranting about the deficit for six and a half years when his government could have actually done something about lowering the deficit, this announcement is absolutely unbelievable. I can hardly wait for the minister's legislation.
Where did the minister's projections go wrong? Why is he so far off? Because the minister and his government have failed to understand that the deficit problem is not simply solved by cutting away at programs, by cutting away at institutions, but by promoting growth and investment which is something they have failed to do. Perhaps it is because of his high interest rate policies. Perhaps it is those high dollar policies.
It is not so easy for the minister to say that the current recession is not as bad as the recession of 1981-1982, which is like comparing apples and oranges. Canadians know the recession of 1981-1982 was an international recession, not as the New Democratic Party Leader

alleged today a Liberal recession, but one emanating from international problems which affected the major industrialized nations. This recession on our hands today, however, we all know is a made-in-Canada recession.
I want to examine some of the features included in the budget and Main Estimates for which this government must get the authority to borrow. The Canadian Jobs Strategy, the government's so-called retraining program, will have its funding slashed by $100 million. It is outrageous.
Since the minister acknowledged in this House that he expects the national unemployment rate to rise above 10 per cent this year, it means that an additional 200,000 jobs will be added to the 1.3 million people who are already out of work in this country. For those Canadians with jobs, the Conservative government has raised unemployment insurance. We warned them about Bill C-21. Premiums are up.
I would like to go on with all the examples that I have in this budget. There have been job cuts. In Hamilton West and environs I will give a few examples of companies. A year ago January we had an unemployment rate in Hamilton of 4.7 per cent. Just last January, one year later, it climbed to 8.8 per cent. In fact, we have had an increase in welfare roles of 46 per cent, but the government wants to cut back.
Let me conclude. Obviously we realize the scope and nature of occupational health and the importance of it in this country. I have been pushing day after day in this House about the CCOHS in Hamilton West. In fact, this House approved re-instituting funding to that organization. It has fallen on deaf ears with the minister.
Instead of investing in preventive health care, this government is divesting itself of universal health care. Under the guise of providing for tomorrow, this government is methodically dismantling our yesterday, the foundation on which this country was built.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate on the borrowing bill which flows directly from the budget of the Minister of Finance is a very timely debate. I say that because Canadians are very conscious of some of the economic indicators, indicators like the fact that our bankruptcies are up sharply. In the month of January alone they rose in this country 69 per cent. At this time we have about 1.3 million Canadians
unemployed and that figure, according to the Minister of Finance will rise shortly to about 1.5 million people. That is a tragedy on a monumental scale.
Since the free trade agreement came into effect we have lost maybe 250,000 manufacturing jobs. That is like a scorched earth policy of a kind. Plants closed. Since Christmas, since the imposition of the GST, retail sales in this country have gone flat. In fact they have gone more than flat; they have gone straight down the tube. Of course, we have inflation shooting up as well and that is attributable also to the GST.
I have one more economic indicator. There are over
180,000	Canadians lining up at food banks in the last year. Something which I find traumatic is that one in six Canadian children is going to bed hungry every night. It is hard to believe that this is Canada when we cite those numbers.
Then under this government and according to this very religious right wing agenda which is pursued with alacrity and enthusiasm, we have seen a diminution of our institutions, be it the CBC, VIA Rail or Canada Post and of course medicare, which I will talk about in a few moments.
Perhaps the most overriding concern, perhaps the major concern in this country and the major preoccupation of Canadians, is how to get rid of this Prime Minister. Really the major questions Canadians ask themselves are: How do we get rid of this Prime Minister? How do we get rid of this government? How do we get rid of a Prime Minister who construes that a five-year mandate given to him through an election of a Parliament as a dictatorship. He can do whatever his little heart desires. Whatever his little old heart desires, he will have. He will not listen because, after all, he has been given this five-year mandate.
Mr. Speaker, when was the last time that you or that gentleman over there, or the other gentleman over there, was asked how to impeach a Prime Minister? Is there a way of impeaching a Prime Minister of Canada? Unfortunately I have to say that I know of no way we can impeach a Prime Minister. There is a way of getting rid of a Prime Minister. There is the old-fashioned political process, but I do not know of a way to impeach a Prime Minister. Yet, if I have been asked that question once, I
March 5, 1991

have been asked that question a thousand times: How do you impeach a Prime Minister?
Canadians are perplexed by our system. I will tell you why. They look across the pond over to Great Britain and they see how easy it was to get rid of a Prime Minister who had served beyond her time. There was a time when Margaret Thatcher was riding high, particularly after the Falklands War. She was untouchable, she was unbeatable, but the Iron Lady had served her time. They had a very simple way of getting rid of that Prime Minister. It was almost painless.
I think Canadians ask themselves: Why don't we have something like that? Why do we have to live with this monstrosity that hangs around our neck? Why do we have to live with a Prime Minister who has absolutely no moral authority to govern, a man who has been sitting in the polls at 14, 15 and 16 per cent?
Here is a man who says: "I will do whatever I want, regardless of public opinion and regardless of what Canadians want". Be it Meech Lake, the GST or the war in the gulf, it does not matter. This Prime Minister absolutely refuses to comply or to heed for one moment what Canadians are saying.
That is why Canadians are perplexed. They ask themselves about something as unpopular as the GST. There were 80 to 85 per cent of Canadians who did not want that tax. How many Tories said: "We will vote against this government and we will vote against the tax"? None, except two who were expelled from the caucus.
Canadians asked themselves: Why, when there is such an unpopular tax measure, can we not get backbenchers on the government side to stand up and vote according to their conscience? It is very simple: Because they know that under our system if they vote down the government, they vote down themselves; if they kill the government, they kill their own political careers.
So they stay like good little boys and girls, because they do not want to lose their political careers. I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, Canadians are absolutely fed up with it. The party system or the party discipline has gone too far. Particularly on the government side of the House, an MP is a mere puppet.
The cabinet does not have to earn its legislation. Once the cabinet stands up and says "this is the way it is going
Government Orders
to be", what do the government MPs do? They are just like seals and puppets. All they say is: "Yes, sir; no, sir."
Canadians are absolutely fed up with it, right up to the teeth, and they will not put up with any more. Mark my words: there are going to be many Tory MPs who will pay the ultimate price because they would not represent their constituents.
I do not think I have any time left, but let me say something that relates directly to the budget. The finance minister and in fact all cabinet ministers go around and say: "We are not touching medicare, this crown jewel of social programs in this country". They are not touching it, despite the fact that they are going to take $2.3 million out of EPF, that is out of transfer payments to the provinces.
The estimates show clearly in black and white that the reduction in medicare payments will be in excess of $1 billion. Yet, these people have the unmitigated gall to say: "Oh, no, we are not touching medicare. Don't worry about it. Everything is fine and dandy".
The fact of the matter is that in just a handful of years there will be no more cash payments from the federal Treasury to the provinces for medicare. Yet, they have the gall to say: "Don't worry, we are not hurting medicare".
Once the government moves away from financial support for medicare, it is dead in the water, especially from the point of view that it will no longer be a national program. It will be the rich provinces that will have medicare. The poorer provinces will have a poorer kind of medicare.
I could go on about the slash in job creation programs. I could go on about the 24 per cent increase in UI premiums, which will have a devastating effect on small business. I could tell you, Mr. Speaker, if I had the time that there is absolutely nothing in this budget for rural Canada.
There is $1.3 million for the agricultural community, and I am very thankful for that. However, let me point out that $1.3 billion is supposed to cover the farm safety-net programs, GRIP and NISA, but that does not cover $300 to $900 million for the deficit of the Canadian Wheat Board. It does not cover the $450 million which is the shortfall in payments under the Western Grain

This budget is a failure. It is a failure. It is a Tory budget. You had better believe it. It is a Tory budget and it is a failure and Canadians understand that very well.

But I want to tell the hon. member something. As he pointed out some have left, some did not agree with this government, just as people have left his own party during the last 12 months and sat elsewhere. But let me tell him
that those of us who sit here sit here because we are proud to serve under a leader who has the courage to do what is right for Canada, who has the courage to be on the side of right even though it may mean unpopularity from time to time.
I think of the recent events in this world. Where did his party stand? Did they stand by the right, or did they stand by the polls. Mr. Speaker, Bill C-97, which proposes borrowing another $26.4 billion, is one of a long series of government bills doing this. It is number nine since this particular party became the government in Canada. By this means they have borrowed something in excess of $200 billion, almost one-half of what the total debt of the country is at the present time.
The money is needed. We do not question that it will be needed by the time its authority under this bill runs out, due to the mismanagement of the government in office. For that reason alone, if for no other reason, we will have to vote against it as our expression of just how we feel about the mismanagement of this government.
I had the opportunity to watch the presentation of the budget in the House and made notes of a few things that I would question or that I would have liked to see changed. Of course, one does not get the opportunity to change them, but certainly one does get an opportunity to question.
The Minister of Finance talked throughout his budget about our inability to compete internationally. Well, whose fault is that? It was this minister, in co-operation with the Governor of the Bank of Canada who produced what the Conference Board of Canada called the first made-in-Canada depression, I mean recession. I better use the word recession, I suppose, it is the one they use.
The minister knew how it was accomplished. He kept saying over and over that he had to cool off the over-heated economy in southern Ontario. He did that by increasing interest rates and by increasing the price of the Canadian dollar. It was very simple. He knew exactly what he was doing. He boasted about it. It was the way he was going to do it. And surprise, surprise, it worked. At least that time he was right.
If it works so well to create a recession, then why not use the medicine in reverse to create growth of the economy, prosperity? But he is not ready to do that. He increased interest rates to cool off the economy and instead of bringing them down steadily and more rapidly, he is threatening to stop because he wants to control the growth of inflation. He wants to get the inflation growth
Government Orders
down to 2 per cent. Well, when is he going to start turning the screws again? When are the interest rates going to start going up because we are nowhere near 2 per cent now.
He knows how to do it, but he is not prepared to do it because to him it is far more important to get inflation down to 2 per cent than it is to put Canadian people back to work. It is just that simple.
Was or was not the Canadian dollar part of the free trade deal? A former member of the cabinet of the Conservative government said that it was included in the agreement, not in the documents we read, but that it was part of the deal that our Prime Minister made with the President of the U.S. It would then be easier for the U.S. to export into Canada and make us more of a branch plant economy than we had been then and are now. This government is continuing that process of increasing the Canadian dollar to make it even more difficult for us to compete internationally.
And that is what it was all about. After all, it was the Americans that had a tremendous trade deficit with Canada and it was their desire to turn that around and our desire to co-operate totally with everything that Uncle Sam wanted.
He wants to get the deficit down to $28.5 billion. Well, at least he is consistent. I have heard that same figure every year that I have been here, and I know from previous experience that it was close to that every year before that. So it is always the target, but it is not going to be this year, it is not going to be next year. Two years from now it is going to be $28.5 billion. As I say, he gets full marks for being consistent.
When it comes to pay increases, they are going to be limited. But the part I liked, the part I just had to chuckle at, is that the increases for executives, deputy ministers, heads of Crown corporations, the people who are all at the top of the salary scale now, are going to be limited to the same rate as the rate bargained for with employees subject to bargaining. If they get 3 per cent, for example, then the Governor of the Bank of Canada, who got a 30 per cent increase last year, is going to get 3 per cent on top of whatever he is getting this time. The increase alone will be something like three times what the highest person in the bargaining sector gets as his total salary.

March 5, 1991

That is fairness, according to our Minister of Finance: the same rate. Is that restraint?
The restraint package of this budget adds up to $1.1 billion. The Auditor General told the minister how he could recover more than that in a year, but he chose not to accept the advice. Remember the proposal to impose a new tax on banks because they had not been paying taxes? A favourite story is that a teller in the Royal Bank was paying more taxes than was the Royal Bank. The Minister of Finance was going to get after them and was going to raise $2.5 billion from that one source alone. However, he came into the House two years ago and said that it proved to be too difficult, so we are going to let the banks get away with it; we will not tax them the $2.5 billion they could well afford to pay.
The Auditor General said that over a period of 10 years of the manufacturers' sales tax, the government had forgone $2.4 billion in revenue by not having enough people checking up on the corporations which were paying it. So once again, because it is too difficult to watch the corporations, we will let them get away with that $2.4 billion.
He said also that hiring one more tax auditor at a cost of, say, $40,000, on the basis of the figures he had within the Ministry of Finance, would bring in from $300,000 to $900,000 in extra revenue. For an expenditure of $40,000 there could be additional revenue of $300,000 to $900,000. He said there were hundreds of millions of dollars out there waiting to be picked up that way.
He warned us when we went into the GST program that because we did not have the auditors, because we were not ready to examine the inventories, for example-there were different ways, but one of them was to check the inventories on which the government was going to be paying GST tax credits for manufacturers' sales tax that they would have paid previously-we were possibly losing hundreds of millions of dollars there as well.
The government had the opportunities to go after the corporations and to go after the high income taxpayers; the Auditor General told it where some of them were and it knew where the others were. But it chose to go after the little fellow, as it is doing in limiting the wage increases to the lowest wage earners in the government
sector, limiting them and letting off the people at the top, the high salary earners, the big corporations, the ones with the inventories that are going to make money on the GST when it opens up, because it is difficult to go after the big boys.
Mr. Speaker, he never explained to us why it was difficult to go after the banks for $2.5 billion. The government has never tried to deal with the Auditor General's concern about what should be done to tighten up on controls so that the corporations would not get away with claiming excessive GST credits on inventories; no explanation at all, no attempt to explain any of that, to the best of my knowledge.
The GST is going into a fund to deal with the deficit. I can remember in the legislature in B.C. when I was there four years ago, the Minister of Finance brought in a new fund. He called it "The Budget Stabili2ation Fund". At the time it was thought that it was somebody within his own department who used a name that could be shortened to "BS", because they knew that was exactly what it was and they wanted to reveal it to the world.
This is another "BS" fund. heart in 1987 and went up just slightly, by 3.5 per cent. But then in the following two years dropped it again by 8.5 and 8.3 percentage points.
